Chapter 12. Putting it all together to create an incredible life. Two most important days in your life. The day you were born and the day you discover why. Mark Twain, author. I wrote in the introduction to this book that my goal was to share with you the habits I had observed in my happiest and most successful clients. I hope by now you implicitly realize that when I say successful, I do not simply mean rich, famous and powerful. Success is so much more than that. There are so many people who look outwardly successful but are inwardly impoverished. Indeed, in my 30 years of being a therapist, I've seen that more times than I can count. Successful in this context means something entirely different. It means being your own ally, friend and cheerleader, even when the world or your social network isn't doing that for you. It means seeing the inherent value in building up those around you because you know how to build up yourself. It means knowing that working towards your dreams and goals becomes a lot easier once you have your brain working for you, not against you. It means letting go of the stories and limiting beliefs you've told yourself or being given by your family and embracing the idea that you and you alone are responsible for the words and pictures in your head. It means being kind to others naturally because you're kind to yourself first. What tends to happen when a person does all the things I just described is that they become successful without even trying. They may not have pursued wealth, love and fame so much as they did the inner work to address and change how they think. But when you're happy on the inside, good things tend to happen. What I often find is that people who have the outer trappings of success without the internal work are even more unhappy than those who live more modest lives. But those who have both, outer and inner success are really on top of the world. That's who I want you to be. This observation from my practice and work is backed up by Tony Robbins, author, entrepreneur, philanthropist and life coach, who often talks about the difference between achievement and fulfillment. There are two parts to having an extraordinary life. The first part is mastering the science of achievement. How do I take what I envision and make it real? And how do I do it quicker, faster, better, easier? There are a lot of people who are very good at that and they still don't have an extraordinary life. They have a life that you see as extraordinary. But I get the phone call from the multibillionaire who tells me he is miserable and depressed. The second skill is the art of fulfillment. If you want an extraordinary life you can't just achieve. You've got to be fulfilled. In other words, success without this fulfillment piece of the puzzle will still leave you unhappy. As discussed earlier, this is why so many of the rich and famous among us become addicted, take their own lives, or lose all their money and squander their talents. They pursue and achieve success but neglect the work of fulfillment. And the fact that they still feel unhappy kills them, sometimes literally. You may wonder why it is that so many of us seem to focus on achievement before fulfillment. The answer lies largely in our culture. We are encouraged from a very young age to pursue a rather rigid version of success that is synonymous with money, renown and prestige. Once we get to the age where we are choosing education, jobs and careers, we are more than just encouraged to go after the outer trappings of success but incentivized. While that's not inherently a bad thing, it can become destructive. Because it is most often not paired with the kind of inner work that doesn't result in GDP gains for the global economy or boosting our bank account. For the most part, people pursue external achievement because that's what they see and are taught to do. They ignore inner work because there are fewer models of it and instructions for it. I said earlier in this book that I firmly believe inner work, including self-love and the belief that I am enough, is the kind of material that should be taught in schools, right alongside math, economics and English. I hope that one day this will be the case. But until the idea of fulfillment before achievement becomes more mainstream in our society, I fear that most people will pursue external success first and only reach the fulfillment work far later in life, if ever. It is my sincerest hope that spreading my teachings through books such as this will help popularise that message. If you feel moved to pursue this path of fulfillment after listening to this book and I believe you will, it will lead you to the holy grail of inner work and personal development, your purpose. Finding your purpose. I work with many coaches and train a lot of therapists and by and large the most common thing that individuals come seeking help with from a coach is in finding their purpose or the thing they are meant to be spending their time doing. A purpose is different than a job or a career. Sometimes it may earn you money but other times it does not. A purpose is one thing for everyone though. When you are doing it, you feel complete and total peace in the knowledge that this is what you are meant to be doing. It's true that not everyone in life has the luxury or privilege of finding their purpose. They may be too focused on survival or they may have the burden of taking care of others. But if you are listening to this book, I suspect it's because you know that you have a purpose to find and enact throughout your life and you are likely lucky enough to find a purpose. You do not want to become one of the many people who have this feeling and do not honour it. Those people are, after all, the most depressed people in our world. So, how can a person find this purpose if they are not sure what it's supposed to be? Here is a clue. Your purpose very often has a direct relationship with whatever you love to do between the ages of about seven. Why those ages? Well, at seven you are old enough to begin to develop your own sense of self. And at 14 we begin to internalise the pressures and insecurities of the world around us. And perhaps start moderating our behaviour accordingly to fit in or be good. But between those two ages we find a sweet spot where we were allowing our desires and passions to direct how we spent our time. Now, you might think, but at eight years old all I love doing was twirling and dancing. Or as a 12 year old I spent every spare moment I could in a tree. Of course those things might not be able to pay your mortgage now. But if dancing, movement, spending time outdoors or working with animals are things that excited you then. There's every likelihood they will excite you now too. As I said before our culture unfortunately is very fixated on achievement. We don't think it's worth doing something unless we can be great at it. Or unless it can make us wealthy and adored and famous. But that's not what a purpose is. A purpose is not driven by ego or greed or competitiveness. It is driven by a desire for meaning and being helpful to others. This may not be totally apparent at first. You might think me going to a dance class in middle age is not going to help anyone. But I've found that when people honour what they enjoy doing, their paths start to unfold and progress in mysterious ways. Perhaps one dance class will lead to many more. And you start inspiring your friends to join in. Perhaps you get good enough that you think it might be a good idea to teach your own class free of charge at your local community centre. This may not ever allow you to quit your day job. And that's okay. But the joy you'll feel from living out your purpose in some way will make you view your day job entirely differently. As something that allows you to live your purpose. From all my work with people, I truly believe that the largest cause of depression is failing to follow your heart's desire in a profound and deep way. Don't allow yourself to do this. Even if it seems impractical, unimpressive, small or completely random, find a way to follow your curiosity about your calling. And I can guarantee that wonderful things will unfold. And don't forget, whatever form it may take, when you love what you do, you have purpose. And when you share that purpose, you have meaning. Habits of action versus habits of thought. You'll remember earlier on I delineated the difference between habits of thought and habits of action. Most of us have habits of thought. We are just not aware of them. We indulge in critical self-dialogue without realizing that doing so is a choice. That has a major impact on how we feel and move through the world. In psychology, these inner forces are often called saboteurs. And people allow a range of them to affect their lives. Whether it's the inner judge, the controller, the restless, the stickler, the pleaser, the avoidor, the victim, the hyper-vigilant, the hyper-achiever, or the hyper-rational, these saboteurs can run the show if we allow them. As one researcher from Stanford University found, some of the world's most outwardly successful people are ruled by their various saboteurs. Using negative emotions as fuel to push them, they'll ultimately fall short of their true potential. In other words, while the saboteurs may be helpful in getting you outward success and achievement, via things such as making you a perfectionist, work a hollock, or cutthroat competitor, they will never make you happy if you allow them to rule your mind. Much of the material in the previous chapters is designed to help you overcome these saboteurs using one of two methods, habits of thought and habits of action. I started the book with habits of thought that you can implement in tiny and large ways throughout your life. The first habit of thought was learning that your mind does what it thinks you want it to do. As I explained, the mind is always operating in this fashion, most people just aren't aware of it. If every time you drive to the office you think this is going to be hell, then your brain takes that cue and makes you feel accordingly. However, if you communicate with yourself in a precise, detailed and specific way, your mind will help you move towards your goals rather than sabotaging them. Just as we update our software on our phones and laptops, we have to update the way our brain operates. The next habit of thought was controlling the words and pictures in your head. I explained how babies can't be afraid of flying, even though it's wildly unfamiliar to them, because they haven't learned to associate it with negativity or fear. We were all born with this phenomenal confidence, not just about flying, about everything, but we unlearn it as we grow up. The answer is to lie, cheat and steal. That is to lie to your brain, cheat fear and steal back the confidence you were born with. Even if something fills you with dread or fear, if you replace those images and words with a more neutral one, you can lessen the effect that a given event or occurrence has on you. Remember, a needle is perceived differently by a heroin addict versus a nurse versus someone with a needle phobia. The difference isn't in the needle, but in the perception of it. You and you alone have the power over this perception, so use it. The third habit of thought I taught you in chapter 3 was making the familiar, unfamiliar and the unfamiliar familiar. A frustrating quirk of the brain is that it always craves the familiar, even that which we know isn't helpful to us anymore. It's why diets fail, people choose bad relationship partners and lottery winners lose their money as fast as they can spend it. But it doesn't have to be that way. If you think consciously about what you'd like to make familiar and unfamiliar, you can begin to distance yourself from the bad and move towards the good. If you know the things you tend to move towards and away from, you can begin to intervene before mental habits take over. That's where your real power lies. As I said in chapter 3, if you go to the finish line of a marathon, it's not filled with lifelong runners. It's filled with people who made getting up to run familiar, many of whom used to more commonly sit on the couch. In chapter 4, we switched to a habit of action rather than a habit of thought. I told you that successful people learn not only to do what they hate, but to do what they hate first to get it out of the way. Note that this doesn't mean learning to love doing what you hate. It would be hard to love doing your taxes, for example. But you can learn to love the feeling of accomplishment that comes after doing what you hate and getting it out of the way. We also explored this through the science behind habit formation and that the Q, behavior reward model is a helpful tool you can use for creating new habits and spotting ones you'd like to get rid of. Doing what you hate is not about trudging along in jobs, relationships or activities you hate, but rather a way to get through life's more mundane but necessary tasks and feel better for it. Chapter 5 explored another habit of action. Taking action in the direction of your goals each and every day. This is less about becoming a workaholic and working seven days a week. That isn't sustainable anyway. And more about establishing a pattern of working towards success on a daily basis, even if it's just for five or ten minutes. This can take many forms from meditation to sending out pitches. But the point is to work with the idea that your mind is a goal seeking missile. It wants something to move towards. As I like to say, in life there are no shortcuts but there are guarantees. If you do one thing each day in the direction of your dream, it's guaranteed you'll get close to it. Chapter 6 gave us another habit of action. Delaying gratification. We spoke about the famous Stanford marshmallow experiment where the children that were able to delay a sweet treat grew up to become more successful and well adjusted adults. While the children in the experiment may have naturally possessed that trait, you don't have to. If you begin structuring your day and tasks around rewards big and small, you can teach yourself to delay gratification and enjoy its benefits. This can apply to everything from your diet to your biggest goals in life. It also applies to parenting. I shared with you how I've learned from my clients that people who give their children everything rob them of the ability to delay gratification on a long term. These children often end up very unhappy as they are resentful they never got the chance to feel the kind of accomplishment and satisfaction that goes along with achieving your goals after working hard, which is another form of delayed gratification. Remember whether it's savoring your favorite coffee after writing a difficult email or not going on holiday until you finished your book manuscript. It is in the earning of something that we feel good, not the mere attainment of it. In Chapter 7 we talked about how we can apply different habits of thought and action to something that affects so many people. We also covered the idea that repairing your relationship with food and your body doesn't just mean changing how you think about yourself, but changing how you think about the environment that we are operating in. Once we remember we are cavemen wandering around a grocery store filled with sugar and fat, we make different choices about what to buy. In Chapter 8 we explored what I believe is the most important habit of thought you can possibly integrate into your life, the belief that you are enough. Everyone is born into the world knowing that they are enough. The source of that phenomenal confidence that babies possess which we discussed in Chapter 2. Then somewhere along the way people learn that they aren't enough. This can happen in so many ways. Maybe their mother desserts them, leading them to believe they're not lovable. Or maybe they get teased in school, leading them to believe they'll never be liked unless they are thin. The belief of not feeling enough manifests in myriad ways, addiction, workaholism, suicide, mental health problems etc. But all those reasons are connected. Not feeling enough, I believe, is the biggest disease affecting humanity. The good news is you don't have to spend years and years in therapy undoing it. You and you alone can convince yourself you are enough with the power of the simple, affirmative phrase, I am enough. The more you say it, the more you believe it, even if at the beginning it feels futile. I've seen it change the lives of so many people and I know it can change yours too. In Chapter 9 we learned one more habit. This one is a combination of both action and thought, to let in praise and reject criticism. As a habit of action this is rather straightforward, when someone gives you a compliment, don't deflect it, but rather say thank you and let it in. When someone is out to hurt you through harsh criticism, use the tactics described in the chapter to deflect it. And most importantly, know that they're drive to critique you comes from their own unhappiness. When it comes to the habit of thought, praising yourself, this is something few people know the power of. Praising yourself and telling yourself the things you need to hear in order to feel good is a habit that so many happy people I've worked with share. Learning to make your inner dialogue match how you would speak to a good friend will do wonders for your productivity, confidence and quality of life. You don't have to wait for others to praise you to feel good about yourself. Praise yourself today and every day. Finally in Chapter 10 we learned how loving one's self is the most vital ingredient to loving another. Often bad relationships are a sign of two people who don't love themselves first. And then we also learned that once you find that sustaining relationship, committing to an active and fantasy-filled sex life is a vital and fun way to maintain it. You may have noticed that throughout the chapters we've reviewed above there were several recurring themes that apply to each habit of thought or action. These themes are important as understanding them will fill your toolbox with ways to hold onto these lessons and implement them in your daily life. It's easy to read a book after all, but changing your habits and thoughts requires a little bit of work. The first and most important theme you need to remember is the power of repetition. Every single tactic I've outlined in each chapter works only if you repeat it and repeat it often. As I mentioned before it takes a minimum of 10 days and a maximum three weeks to completely let go of an old belief. Crucially it takes the same amount of time to create a new one. Often when people begin to implement the tactics I advise, they come back to me saying, how do I know if it's working? Or I tried it a couple of times it didn't work. What these people are missing is that the power of repetition is cumulative. It's not an instant flash of change, but rather a slow and gradual nudging of our brain to a more positive and productive place. Often the shift is imperceptible. When trying the tactics outlined in the book, I urge you to have persistence and stick with them for at least three weeks before you judge the effect they're having on you. We repeat negative habits all the time without knowing it. Sometimes it takes replacing them with positive habits for them to really stick. Though I've been a therapist for 30 years, the truth is that a lot of what I teach flies in the face of the conventional wisdom of the field. I don't advise that you spend months and years sitting in a therapy chair talking about your feelings. On the contrary, I believe in locating the source of my clients pain quickly and then helping them reform their beliefs in a rapid and transformational way, using the kind of tactics and habits outlined in this book. That said, I get many readers who come to me with a lot of emotional pain and hurt that they feel they can't undo themselves. They wonder if, perhaps, they need a longer stint of therapy to get to the bottom of it. While everyone is different, the truth is simple. You can't undo your past, but what you can do is change your narrative about it. Talking about your past for years in a therapy chair stops being useful if you're not replacing the hurt and pain with a new narrative. While therapy can be helpful in finding that new narrative, it's rarely required to sit in a therapy chair indefinitely to do this. Many of our issues can be complex, but the way to overcome them never has to be complex. It can be fast, effective and transformational. That is always my preferred method of therapy. Once you've located the issues that are underpinning your behaviors, it's time to change how you frame or feel about those issues. The only person who can do that is you. We are here for such a short time, and I truly believe that life is an immense gift. I have watched clients, readers and followers of mine from all over the world change their lives in an instant. How? Because they change their thoughts and beliefs. No matter who you are or what you've gone through, you have the power to change your thoughts and beliefs too. I truly believe that through your thoughts, actions and habits, you can begin to do so today and every day. I can't wait to hear about your transformation. Prolog Is it possible that our deepest pain stems from the lies we tell ourselves? Why does therapy have to take so long? Why does it require the client to spend months forming a relationship with the practitioner before any healing happens? If someone is in pain, whether it's physical or emotional, shouldn't they receive urgent intervention to provide pain relief as soon as possible? These questions have percolated within me ever since I became a therapist in 1984. My clients would turn up in my office suffering from severe long-term pain that stemmed from low self-esteem, extreme fears and phobias, and myriad addictions. Had these clients turned up in the emergency room or at the dentist or chiropractor in physical pain, they would have been offered immediate treatment. I understood that clients often form long-term relationships with their therapists, but I did not understand why those same clients had to wait so long before getting some relief. It seemed that all pain hurt, but not all pain was treated equally. When my clients turned up in tears, suffering panic attacks or extreme sadness and depression, I wanted to help them as fast as I possibly could. To do that, I needed to both understand the origin of their issue and teach them how to be free of it. Einstein said to simplify, simplify, simplify, so I decided to create a new brand of therapy, rapid transformational therapy, to help my clients and the people listening to this book get better and faster results. We can't get better without knowing what we know and feeling what we feel. My own clients were the driving force behind this. After enough instances where I heard feedback such as, you changed my life, or I have been in therapy for years but what you did was so much faster and more effective. I decided I must make my method of therapy more widely available. I knew I needed to do this not just by training therapists in my method, but also by explaining how people can use my techniques to heal themselves at home. So many people don't have the money or the time to attend long term therapy, and for some people, there is still a stigma attached to seeing a therapist. I wrote this book to give the reader valuable insight and tools and arm them with the self-knowledge to live a better, more fulfilled life. Let's get started. Several chapters in this book mention or deal with thoughts of suicide. If you are feeling vulnerable or are in need of immediate support, never hesitate to seek help. In the UK, Samaritans can be reached at 116-123. In the US, the National Suicide Prevention Hotline is 1-800-273-8255. Both can be reached 24 hours a day, 7 days a week. For a list of international numbers, search Wikipedia for List of Suicide Crisis Lines.

Introduction Everyone has a story to tell. It's a sentiment so obvious that it almost sounds cliche, but having been a therapist for more than 30 years, working with everyone from major celebrities and athletes to successful business titans, I know that the stories people tell other people about themselves are not the most important ones. People have come into my offices in Los Angeles and London and told me the most extraordinary stories over the years. They've told me how they ruin their lives with addiction, how they just can't stop shopping even though their credit card debt is crippling, how they have everything they've ever dreamed of having, and yet they are still miserable. They've told me how they are incapable of not ruining relationships through infidelity, how heartbroken they are that it seems impossible for them to have a baby, or how their rigid obsessive compulsive disorder is ruining their ability to have friendships or relationships with anyone. To these clients, these stories feel true. In fact, they don't even feel like stories they are just plain reality. However, if we were being a little blunter, we might say that the stories people tell about themselves are actually lies, or at the very least they are simply one version of events. We begin to change our lives when we realise that the stories we tell ourselves can change too. That's the thing about stories. They are not fixed entities. While there are certain facts that remain unchanged, the way we frame those facts can change over time. Just ask any tabloid journalist, man enters house, may be a fact. But if you attach a motivation for why the man entered the house, so lies what he was thinking while he did it, and even speculate about what he did after he left the house, then you have a story, and often in the tabloids a highly contestable one. We learn these stories throughout our lives, however the ones we learn as small children tend to root down deeply into our psyche. At the root of these stories are fundamental beliefs about who we are, and what we are capable of. And unfortunately, we can develop these beliefs through adverse experiences, or our parents or caretakers unresolved traumas and issues. One of those core beliefs that I see over and over is that a child believes they are not lovable and not enough. When that destructive belief takes root, that child will take it with them, often unknowingly, into every single interaction and relationship for the rest of their life. That unmet need to feel lovable and enough will colour the rest of their life if it's not eventually resolved. It is these fundamental beliefs that morph into stories and eventually lies people tell themselves. Someone may walk into my office and say, every single time a relationship I'm in gets serious, the person leaves after just under one year. I make such horrible decisions about partners. I'll always be alone. The belief at the core of that story may be, my father left me and my mother when I was an infant, so I'm obviously not lovable. Another story might sound like, I'm addicted to cookies and sugar, and I am absolutely powerless to stop eating them, even though they are ruining my life. I may find through RTT that the belief at the source of that is, I was sexually abused as a child, and I have to keep myself safe by being big. Those beliefs are so powerful, get people walk throughout life, not even knowing they have them. You'll hear me say this several times throughout this book. No one has a perfect childhood. However, some people are lucky enough to get by with an okay enough story. They fundamentally feel a sense of belonging and safety that allows them to move through life productively, if not with some bumps in the road. But other people inherit stories about themselves that deeply harm their ability to live functional, healthy lives with meaningful relationships with themselves and others. They may try all kinds of things, shopping, alcohol, work, sex, money, etc. to drown out the painful truth of their story that they are not enough. Not good enough, smart enough, attractive enough, interesting enough, worthy enough, that they are not lovable, that they don't deserve to be happy, that they are not safe, that their needs will never be met because they are unworthy. But as you may have gathered by now, none of those methods actually work. They only prolong one of two inevitable outcomes, transformation or destruction. After 30 years of private practice, I created rapid transformational therapy, RTT, because it was clear to me that so much of the pain and suffering we see in the world comes down to the fundamental stories we tell ourselves and how often those stories are untrue or outright lies. The personal development industry, as well as the traditional talk therapy in general, is often presented as a lifelong process, one where people are asked to start at the present day and slowly peel away the layers of themselves in order to figure out why they are so unhappy, destructive, depressed or dysfunctional. But in my decades of being a therapist, I saw far too many clients who were way past that point. They didn't have months or years to figure out how to fix what was wrong with them. They could barely see a way to survive until next week. It was in those sessions with clients who were on the brink of suicide or total self-destruction that I began to devise the methods I will present in this book. So how do we do it? How can people whose lives have been ruined by an incorrect story or lie changed their lives? They have to be willing to change the story, to tell themselves a better lie. At its core, RTT is a highly effective way to get people to do just that. The main reason it works, I believe, is that it overcomes the high level of resistance that most people have to changing fundamental beliefs about themselves by getting to the deepest core of their belief very quickly. It does this using the power of hypnosis. Instead of starting with a 55-year-old addicts' life and working backward through all the woeful and painful things they have undoubtedly been through, we strive to quickly identify the fundamental belief system at the core of their addiction. Often this is a belief that they have been expertly covering up or not acknowledging for decades since childhood. By using it as a starting point rather than an end goal, RTT invites the client to change much faster. Are people resistant to change? Absolutely. However, one of the amazing things about RTT is that people immediately recognize its power. In a therapy office, a client may expertly deflect, dodge and obscure the truth in order to prevent the therapist from getting to the painful core, they've been avoiding their entire life. After all, it can hurt and be quite scary to go deep. But RTT dives right in as quickly as possible. To the client, it immediately feels real, transformational and different. The promise of lasting change comes up front, not after 18 months of sessions. For people who have been suffering due to the destructive lies they've been telling themselves, that much more immediate progress often jolts them into a place of change. It promises relief. At the core of RTT is the belief that no matter what a person's issues are and trust me, I really have seen it all. The solution is the same for everyone. Change the story. Tell yourself a better version of the lie that has been running your life. Sure, change can be scary. People become very attached to the lies that they tell themselves, despite them being so destructive and unhelpful. We underestimate the extent to which the human mind loves what's familiar. But the second part of RTT is immediately introducing a better, more compassionate and all-encompassing story. One that is just as powerful but has the opposite effect in terms of outcome. This method enables clients to think differently about their future, after facing and releasing their past. There is a beautiful notion that I detailed in my last book, I am enough, mark your mirror, change your life. The power of this idea lies in its simplicity. I am enough. You are enough. Every single person on the planet is enough, no matter what has happened to them. Everyone deserves to be loved and valued. Stripping away people's destructive lies and implanting this far more generous and empowering story changes everything. As we will explore further in this book, this mantra of I am enough lies at the core of all my teachings and indeed this therapeutic method. There is nothing I am more passionate about than spreading this idea. It's been an honor to watch so many people's lives change in front of my eyes using RTT, and the best news is that thanks to my growing class of practitioners and readers and listeners like you, the transformation is just getting started. What is RTT? It's a fair question to ask just what rapid transformational therapy is and how it differs from other therapeutic methods. In many ways as a therapist, I've always been a little unconventional. Back when my private one-to-one practice was particularly active, I had a reputation for being a therapist's therapist. As many fellow practitioners would send me their most intractable clients, in the hope I'd once again be able to find a way forward. I usually did. I also became known for solving many of my clients' issues in just one to three sessions, which goes heavily against the grain of the conventional wisdom that you have to slowly build a client's trust before they can really let you you in and be vulnerable. I just never found such a slow process to be necessary or particularly helpful. Where other therapists try to be a blank slate, to be neutral and to follow a strict protocol, I do not. My approach is to be tenacious, resilient and a little bit intuitive. I start from the premise that the clients can help themselves because I truly believe the core truth that serves as the basis of these methods, that every single person is enough, is a life-changing belief that everyone can instill in themselves. I've seen it happen too many times to think otherwise, but the beautiful thing is when you start from the premise that there is an answer and a solution, you can allow the client to lead you to it. While I may be tenacious, I am never domineering or demanding of a client. They lead the way to their own healing, and my job is to help facilitate that. In essence, RTT is the culmination of my life's work, taking influences from modern psychology, psychotherapy, hypnotherapy, healing, counseling and coaching. While I have a deep respect for these more traditional approaches, I wanted to simplify therapy to make it faster, more efficient and more solution-oriented for everyone. Albert Einstein said to simplify, simplify, simplify. So I did. It will come as no surprise to you that clients want rapid help when they are in pain. It is really no different than going to the emergency room and saying, I'm in so much pain, please help me. Imagine if the physician then said, we need to talk about this every week while building up a relationship that allows you to trust me before I can relieve your pain. That would be absurd. When we are in pain of any kind, we wish to be free of it as fast as possible. RTT operates from the belief that emotional and psychological pain require fast and incisive intervention, just as an emergency room doctor would treat pain. But how does RTT do that so quickly when other therapy takes years? In my mind I have worked with has helped me to develop my foundational method of RTT, based on a deep analysis of my most troubling cases and stunning turnarounds. I believe it works because rather than treating clients presenting symptoms, RTT is designed to extract the root cause of every client's issues as soon as possible. After long history of practice, I observe that none of my clients were born with negative beliefs and habits. They acquired them somewhere along the way. RTT rapidly and permanently removes limiting beliefs and habits by exploring with the client how, where and when they acquired them and then helping each client understand and reframe the beliefs that hurt them and held them back. That last part is crucial in the process of removing their pain. RTT also helps them understand where it comes from, which means it won't come back again. Clients see RTT as a worthy investment because they get exactly what they want, freedom from the painful problems of their past. It has always been my passion and drive to simplify therapy. Indeed a big part of RTT's power, both for clients receiving it and practitioners training in it, comes from its simple language. While the technique and methodology of RTT is sophisticated, cutting edge and highly developed, the terminology makes its delivery simple to understand and implement and more accessible for clients. The complex and often technical medical language used in many therapy and hypnosis programs is not accessible or understood by many clients. RTT never speaks in a language that is alien to the client or uses any jargon. Instead it uses a language that the client intuitively understands, so they feel comfortable sharing their story instead of confused or inhibited. So many people approaching therapy already feel a deep sense of shame or feel inferior or misunderstood in life. I believe they should never feel like this in the company of their therapist, rather they should feel understood. One of RTT's most powerful tools is the line of questioning used to elicit what has happened to the client and, just as important, how they feel and what they believe about what happened. It is designed to rapidly uncover what lies beneath the client's feelings and behaviours and then fast-track and awareness for the client. But also, crucially, it ensures that the client leads the way. How I achieve this is something of a delicate art that I discuss in detail during my training. However, as a rule, I always allow the client to tell the scene or story that's on their mind with little interruption or shaping of the narrative. While I don't prompt them on the details of the scene, I do prompt them to come up with the feelings that scene created. So the client might say, I'm six years old and I feel scared and alone. And then I ask them to repeat that sentence adding the word because. Here are some examples of how that might sound. I'm six years old and I feel scared and alone because. Because my mum isn't here, she's at work. I guess work is more important to her than me. This statement may be followed by the realization that the client feels, I need to be better. Maybe then she will spend time with me. Or perhaps the answer that comes is, because my mum and dad are fighting and I can't protect my mummy so I feel small and helpless. This may be followed by, if only I was big, I could protect her. A third response to that prompt may be, because I can't tell my mum I'm being bullied because she's ill and I mustn't worry her. This may be followed by, I'm not worthy of protection and love. By asking them to complete phrases or sentences like those, I'm helping them find the emotional truth that lies at the core of the memory. Hypnosis has been criticized in the past for implanting false early life memories in people. Specifically, the critique has been that leading a client to recall scenes from their early life can unearth false memories, such as abuse that never happened. However, by allowing the client to lead me and believing they know where to go, we can go straight to the storyline that's affecting them, even if it's not a perfectly accurate memory. I know this works because as you'll hear in the dialogue later in this book, clients often push back when I prompt them with a belief or emotion that doesn't feel quite right to them. As a rule, in RTT we always go where the client leads, so when they push back or say, no, that's not how it felt. I allow them to correct course and take us in the direction they're feeling wants to go. One thing that's often misunderstood about my method of RTT is that we can never prove if the exact memories brought up when we do root cause work in hypnosis are 100% accurate or unimpachable. Similarly, it would be difficult to prove that the childhood memories brought up in a regular therapist's office will remember perfectly and accurately. Marissa, and I need to take care of her because... Carry, because no one else will. Carry and I continued our session in this way. I asked her twice more to reveal the role and purpose of the OCD. As painful as it was for her, it was so important and revealing to work this way, and for the client, it's powerful. I'm a great believer in the idea that you can't heal what you don't feel. Somewhat unfortunately, you have to feel it in order to understand it, and therefore heal it. But even though that's painful, in that understanding comes a phenomenal transformation that enables you to let go. Carry went on to say that her OCD must look after her because no one else did. She revealed that the OCD kept her away from the world and thus kept her safe. As I said at the beginning of this chapter, it makes logical sense. If no one can get to her because she is constantly busy keeping clean, cocooned in her bathroom, then in a way she is safe from the kinds of abuse she experienced as a child. Specifically this sexual abuse she reported experiencing at such a young age. Of course it makes the most sense in the world that a five or six-year-old child couldn't possibly cope with the trauma and confusion of sexual abuse on her own. But for an adult, it was important for Carry to make sense of the memory and recast it. While it can be painful to do so, it is not to make her suffer. The goal is for the client not to relive the memories but to review them objectively with a new lens. I often encourage clients to review painful events with a sense of fascination for how people behaved and how that behaviour shaped them. They weren't in control then but they can regain control now. The beautiful thing is if the client is able to do that, they can begin to set themselves free. They might say, oh yeah, I see now what caused that and while it was painful, it was also painful to see what my mind came up with because it's my mind and now I'm in control here, I can stop it. The goal in Carry's case was to make her see that she actually did not need the OCD anymore. She is not the five-year-old child being abused who needs to rest back control in some way. She is an adult with much more power over her own safety. More importantly, she is a grown woman who is capable of loving herself. Not one who needs to rely on inconsistent and distracted parents and caretakers to do it for her. Carry learns to parent herself. The next step with Carry was crucial. She needed to see that the OCD was an outdated way to serve her needs. Of course that required her to feel a deep inner sense of safety and love. It also required her to heal the wounds her parents gave her by not showing adequate love and and care for her and not making her feel safe enough to reveal her abuse. It may seem like all that would be impossible to fix in a single session like this. After all, people spend entire lifetimes trying to heal those kinds of fundamental attachment wounds. Not being loved and accepted as a young child shapes the lives of so many adults today and causes many of the world's problems as a result. But at this moment, Carry was incredibly open. She had just reviewed and felt all the incidents that had effectively been ruining her life. Thus it was the perfect time to recast the story that had been underpinning those events to something that served her much better. I invited Carry to thank her OCD for trying to love her, protect her, and keep her safe, and then to release it by telling the habit she didn't need it now. But how could she replace it? It's a myth that the only place we can receive love and acceptance is from our parents. While that certainly is the primary place we are supposed to receive it, lots of factors from intergenerational trauma to societal problems can get in the way as they did in Carry's life. But the beauty of giving yourself a new story is allowing that love and acceptance to come from yourself. That's what I did with Carry. I gave her powerful and suggestible mind something else to focus on. Instead of Carry controlling her personal hygiene with a rigorous routine, what if she directed that energy to controlling her thoughts? Or to telling herself that her inner child was so safe and secure because the person taking care of her, the person ensuring she didn't get mistreated, was the adult Carry. To do this we use the RTT technique called becoming a loving parent where the client addresses their younger self directly and tells their own inner child that things are different now. Our powerful and healing exchange went like this. Marissa, I want you to put your arms around that beautiful little girl. That's it. That sweet little girl who was all alone in the shed, all alone when her mother was getting them ready for photos, all alone when she felt no one liked her. I want you to take that little girl and I want you to take her back to your home in Utah and I want you to say to that little girl out loud, I'm becoming a loving parent to you now. Carry to her younger self, I'm becoming a loving parent to you now. Marissa, say no one in the world can play this role like I can. Carry, no one in the world can play this role like I can. Marissa, I love you exactly the way you are, I love you completely and unconditionally. Carry, I love you exactly the way you are, I love you completely and unconditionally. Marissa, I'm here to protect you and I will always have time for you. Carry, I'm here to protect you and I will always have time for you. Marissa, I will always love you. Carry, I will always love you. Marissa, and I want you to take that little girl out of the shed, out of the family home and I want you to take her back to your home in Utah. You live in a beautiful place, a spiritual place and I want you to walk her through the door wherever you live now and I want you to say you live here with me and I'm upgrading you into my world, to a nicer safer better place. Carry, you live here with me and I'm upgrading you into my world, to a nicer safer better place. Marissa, all the love you've wanted your whole life. Carry, all the love you've wanted your whole life. Marissa, is here with me. Carry, is here with me. Marissa, but from today you see it. Your eyes are clear and you see that you are deeply, powerfully, extraordinarily lovable. I want you to practice saying to that little girl all the things you wanted to hear when you were a little kid. What Carry's story teaches us, all children have the same needs and rights. They need to feel safe, they need to feel loved, they need to be protected, to feel significant and they need to be taken care of. Every child on the planet has those needs and when those needs aren't met the child goes through life trying to get those needs met in a variety of ways, sometimes perverse or harmful. However, this thought process is not explicit, it's sub-intellectual. No child can rationalize such a hurtful thing. They can't simply think, oh my parents are crazy, I'm not safe here what a shame. A child will think, this feeling is so wrong and unbearable. Something is very wrong, I must be crazy, it's my fault. And then they try to change. They may change it with extreme good behaviour like perfectionism or bad behaviour like acting out in violence or self harm. Or they may change it with OCD. The form the behaviour takes will vary depending on the child but the reasoning is the same. But changing themselves won't fix the problem because it's not their fault. So they enter this loop of learned helplessness I mentioned before. I can't fix it but I must but I can't but I must. I'm helpless and hopeless because I can't fix it. It's not at all surprising that this kind of person creates something else they can fix like checking the other million times switching off the lights 100 times cleaning their teeth or combing their hair repeatedly or doing something in one direction. It's a never-ending task but it's one they can actually perform and complete. It makes them feel less helpless. Carrie was a little girl who felt sad, different and unliked. She felt as though everyone wanted to harm her. People on the street, her own brother, her own siblings, even her own mother who harmed her with her indifference and disinterest every day. So she created the OCD to feel safe, loved and protected. What we can learn from her story is truly one of the most important and widely applicable lessons of RTT. The sad truth is that most people in the world to some extent have an experience like carries. While it may not be as severe or obvious to take the form of debilitating OCD, there are so many children in the world who feel a lack of love at a young age. It's a bit of a fairy tale that most people are born with loving parents who look after them and then they repeat that dynamic with their own children. If that were the case most therapists would probably be out of business. Indeed most people experience some trauma, rejection or lack of security as a young child. This is often because parents repeat dynamics that they learned as children and they have not done or had access to the personal work that helps them break that cycle. It would be easy to feel incredibly depressed by this. How is the world supposed to fix its problems if we're all just acting on the hurt of our damaged childhoods? But that is where the greatest hope rushes in. The truth is that while it is ideal for our parents to provide us with the unconditional love, support and security we all deserve as our birthright, it is not the only place we can get it. In fact, we can train ourselves to provide that love and support for ourselves. In effect we can become our own loving parent as adults through extending consistent and unconditional kindness, care and compassion to ourselves. We can teach and assure our wounded scared inner child that they are now safe with us. Once we meet that unmet need, all the behaviors that have developed over a lifetime to cope with this rejection become less necessary. The thing the child was always craving is fulfilled by the adult and crucially no one can take it away. This requires someone like Carrie to have the courage to break that cycle of pain by facing the pain head on. As coach Steffi Wagner elegantly put it, pain travels through families until someone is ready to feel it. That is precisely what Carrie has done. People have a lot of skepticism when they hear that they can heal themselves by simply giving themselves the love they deserve. And I understand that, in a way it sounds too good to be true. In addition much of mainstream therapy is so focused on the manifestation of the problem. So they see a client who has OCD or anxiety and they treat the behavior perhaps with cognitive behavioral therapy or even medication. But before they hand over those pills, they don't usually consider the role that this illness or manifestation is playing in the person's life. They don't ask what unmet need it is meeting. On the other hand, RTT is interested in the function of an ailment illness or behavior. Once we know that, we can feel that unmet need in a more fundamental way rather than treating its present day manifestation. In Carrie's case, becoming a loving parent to herself also meant for giving her parents to some degree. It meant understanding they simply couldn't or didn't meet her needs. But the fact that she can now meet her own needs means it's easier to let them go. Through hypnosis we can say, I wanted your love. I needed your love, but I don't now. I feel compassion for you, but I don't need your love because I can give it to myself. This has such beautiful knock-on effects. People who love and accept themselves at a fundamental level and have compassion for their inner child and the parents who mistreated that child attract so much more love in their lives. They don't walk around partnering up with people who repeat their parents' dynamic. Instead, they attract people who mirror their own self-love and in turn they are more equipped to pass on that deep self-love to their own children if they have them. In RTT terms, I break this process down into three techniques that can be used in succession or on their own depending on the client. The first one you've already read about, becoming a loving parent. That's usually but not always followed by upgrading the child and merging the child with the person the client has become today. Becoming a loving parent is simply introducing the idea that even though your parents may have failed you, that doesn't mean your whole life is ruined. Everyone has the power to reclaim that love for themselves and give it to themselves in abundance. It's an idea that can feel silly to skeptics, but that doesn't make it untrue. A client in hypnosis is in the perfect position to receive that wisdom and healing and really let it in. Much of becoming a loving parent to yourself also involves forgiving the parent for being unable to do that for the child. The client develops a deep sense of self-compassion and regard for their own inner child. And once they do that, they are able to release their own parents with compassion for being unable to provide that. The client can do this because they simply don't need their parents anymore. It's wonderfully freeing and healing to realize that we don't have to walk around for our entire lives unhappy and desperately looking for a way to meet our unmet needs, simply because we had parents unable to meet our needs. It's not about erasing or forgetting the pain that they caused. RTT allows us to face that pain in a profound yet safe way and then release ourselves from it. Accepting the truth that we can provide for ourselves what our parents and caretakers couldn't is a radical form of self-healing that I hope all people will come to know. Carrie's progress Just shy of two years after her session with me, Carrie reports that healing has changed her life in profound ways. Not only has her OCD and obsession with being clean disappeared, but Carrie reports that she has not come up with other obsessive habits as a replacement, even during a time when life has been quite stressful. In the past, when life got hard, I would start bringing in other things, other OCD behaviors in addition to the teeth cleaning and showering, she says. So the RTT not only took all those behaviors away, but also the actual stress and anxiety that was connected to those habits. From right after the session with Marissa, I did not have the stress when entering the bathroom. I did not have that brain space anymore. Carrie says that before her understanding of her OCD was that it was a mystery and she didn't consider that it might have connections to what she knew she went through as a child. I didn't even try to search it out or figure out where it had come from, Carrie says. I think as an adult I just accepted that my childhood was what it was. I didn't connect it to my behaviors that were happening. But now I look back and it makes total sense. I felt unloved and very disconnected as a child, and this behavior counted that for a time. As with so many people, the solution to Carrie's issue was becoming her own loving parent to meet the needs that were left unmet as a child. But it's not as though she walks into the the bathroom today and thinks, I don't need to obsessively wash because I'm my own loving parent now. It's much deeper and more subconscious than that. Once her need was met, the habit was no longer useful to her. At that point, the behavior became irrelevant because the underlying pain of that unmet need was no longer present in sight her. We don't all have just one situation in our lives that we need to overcome. So the biggest thing for me has been finding a way of learning and understanding other situations in my life if I need to. And it's been a really good explorative year of being able to figure out stuff for me, Carrie says. More than anything, it's allowed me to think about and connect other things that I think can feel today back to my childhood and it has helped me through that. RTT for me, role, function, purpose and intention, RFPI. Carrie had no idea that her obsessive hygiene habit was serving an emotional purpose in her life. She only wanted to get rid of the habit itself. This is a common situation for many people. They exhibit some repeated behavior they just can't seem to get control of or put a stop to. They focus on the behavior, tricking themselves out of doing it or providing incentives to stop, without thinking about the purpose or function it's serving for them. Perhaps you have a habit, repeated behavior or tendency you'd like to get rid of. If so, it's possible to investigate it using the technique of RFPI, even if you're not in hypnosis as Carrie was. First, do an honest inventory of what the behavior is. It doesn't have to be as extreme as OCD. It can perhaps be over-reading when you get home from work, constantly failing to prepare for your important work meetings or exams even though you intend to, or spiraling thoughts about health symptoms that don't really exist. Notice what feelings come up before, during and after the behavior. Is there a release, a sadness, an anger? In Carrie's case, the feeling was one of protection and safety. While she was performing her cleaning rituals, she felt in control and protected from the bad things. Depending on your preference, you can have the following conversation with yourself out loud or in a journal. Say to yourself, I'm the part of insert name. That's responsible for the insert behavior. And my only role function and purpose is to make insert name feel insert feeling. Don't overthink your response here. Try to answer as instinctively as possible about how the behavior makes you feel. So using the example of over-reading out of the refrigerator after work, I'm the part of insert name. That is responsible for her binge eating straight from the fridge when she gets home from work. My only role function and purpose is to make insert name. Feel full. Once you've landed on how it makes you feel, consider what the opposite of that is. In Carrie's case, the OCD made her feel safe. The opposite of that, of course, is feeling unsafe. So what needed to be addressed wasn't her behavior of repetitive cleanliness. It was her feelings of a lack of safety that stemmed from childhood. In the example of the binge eating, the opposite of full is empty. So you ask yourself what in your life is causing you to feel empty. Is it a lack of satisfaction at your job? A lack of love? The binge eating is just a stand-in, so try to go deeper to find the source of that feeling. Depending on the behavior or issue you are working with, this technique may help you figure out a good replacement for the problematic behavior or its root cause. If you know you are deeply unhappy in your job, then perhaps you need to start making plans to find a new one, rather than hoping that eating endless snacks will fill you up after an unfulfilling day. If drinking a bottle of wine each night is making you feel numb, then ask yourself what in your life is too intense to feel right now. If your behavior is more rooted in childhood or trauma as carries was, you may need some additional help from a professional RTT therapist to work through it, but often identifying a behavior and the purpose it is serving can start to lessen its power over you. So whenever you find yourself doing something you'd rather not be doing, investigate it using RFPI and you can become an RTT detective to help change your own life.

Chapter 2. Ryan One of the things you've learned quickly as a therapist is that you can't always trust the appearance someone presents to the world. A client can walk into your office looking by a large completely functional, but not far underneath that you may find a world of suffering that makes it hard to comprehend how they carry out everyday life. In fact, when people are functioning in society with a high level of pain that they keep just below the radar, it can feel even worse than an acute presenting issue. There is a great sense of isolation felt when a person appears to be okay among their co-workers and to the outside world, but inside is living a world of torment that they feel everyday. Ryan came to me as one of those people. On his intake form, he did something that a lot of clients do. He circled a great many issues he wanted to address using RTT. These included addiction at varying times to alcohol, marijuana, junk food and pornography. Anxiety, depression, childhood problems, relationship problems and work issues, specifically a fear of success. Regarding his struggles with depression and anxiety, Ryan described that there is times in his life being so depressed he curled up into a ball, unable to go to work. He had also contemplated suicide in the recent past due to his depression. Clients like Ryan, who have a range of presenting issues, none of which is so acute it is immediately obvious to the outside world, can sometimes be challenging for therapists to help. It's hard to know where to start. The depression, the addiction, the fear of success. You could spend weeks figuring out how all these presenting issues connect and interplay with one another and then weeks more finding out where they all originate. I knew from years of experience that all of Ryan's issues likely stemmed from the same originating belief. So instead of working our way backward and asking him to describe how all his pain and suffering manifested today and trying to unpick a complex web of problems, I knew my job was to find the source and treat that. Before any hypnosis took place, I did an intake with Ryan to find out about his life. Ryan said his parents did not have a happy marriage. His father left his mother when he got her pregnant and his own family forced him to come back. It's possible that Ryan sensed or felt this rejection while he was still in his mother's womb. Ryan has two siblings who he described as functioning professionally, but just not into relationships at all. It's very helpful to know how a client siblings, if they have any, have turned out in life. I'll often say to clients, how's your brother? Oh, he's an addict. How's your sister? Oh, she's a hot mess. When they begin to describe how each sibling is damaged, that provides some great information. You will know you are dealing with a family that raised people who have been damaged by their childhood. If, on the other hand, they say, my sisters are amazing. My brother's amazing. This was just me. It's only me. It's interesting to work out why that is. Essentially, what you're trying to work out is what this client's unmet childhood needs are and if the parents were able to meet those needs for any of their children. For any person finding out their unmet needs from childhood is a hugely transformative process. As you'll see from the varied stories in this book, how are unmet childhood needs have a way of shaping us as adults, often in some very unhelpful ways. One of the biggest triumphs is figuring out what your unmet childhood needs might be and how to begin to meet them for yourself as an adult. Unlike Carrie, Ryan had many concurrent presenting issues to work out. It was important to establish what Ryan most wanted to fix. It's vital that the client feels a sense of agency over this process so that they can trust you enough to allow hypnosis to bring about their healing answer. So I asked Ryan if I had a magic wand and could solve any problem with it, what would it be? His answer was simple. He wanted freedom from addictions and to live his life to the fullest without self-sabotaging. His answer pointed to one of the ways that RTT is different from other forms of addiction treatment. My clients often say, I don't drink any more but I'm eating tons of chips. I've given up drugs but now I'm just drinking 20 cans of coca-day and eating lots of candy. Or I don't smoke but I'm getting up at five every day to exercise for three hours. In essence, I've given up something but I've got something else. We have to be smart and courageous enough, both as the client and the therapist, to look at what lies beneath the behavior in question rather than settling for switching to a more socially acceptable addiction. That's why the root cause work we do as part of RTT is so essential. I'm always treating more than the presenting problem and I try to locate its emotional cause as quickly as possible. Another thing that Ryan revealed before we went into hypnosis was having a clear sense of who his parents' favourite was when he was a child. This crucial thing is often ignored or downplayed in real life. Parents brush off ideas that they could possibly have a favourite child, saying cliche things like, of course I love all my children equally. But any therapist worth their salt will tell you emphatically that parents do have favourite children, even if they don't consciously realise it, and it greatly affects children's lives. Parents tend to treat each child differently, often without even realising it. There are all kinds of reasons parents might favour one child over another, things that have little to do with the children themselves, but children having a sense that they're not the favourite can hugely affect their own self-worth. It's logical for a child to think it must be their own fault if their dad doesn't like them, leading them to implant the belief they must not be very likable and that they are inadequate. When a parent does not appear to love or value their child, the child does not stop loving their parent, they stop loving themselves. In Ryan's case, not only was he not his father's favourite, he knew his father left his mother while she was pregnant with him. Furthermore, the fact that he experienced different levels of love from each parent was a very confusing state of affairs for a young child. As the therapist, I took note of all this information for the journey we were about to embark on. I had high hopes that Ryan would be receptive to hypnosis because one of his main problems was addiction. It may sound counterintuitive, but addicts often respond best to hypnosis. After all, people like Ryan wouldn't have all these addictions unless they were highly suggestible, meaning he could change his life by giving himself better suggestions about who he was and what he was capable of. Many addicts are beautiful, fragile, sensitive souls and they are often incredibly creative. This can explain why many artists, creatives and musicians in our culture struggle with addiction. Just as they can become inspired and focused enough to create world-changing music or art, they can also become addicted to destructive forces when they give themselves the wrong suggestions. A lot of the work of helping transform people like Ryan is showing them that their high level of suggestibility is a gift, not a burden. Whether it is destructive or generative depends on what or who is doing the suggesting. We wanted Ryan to give himself better suggestions to live the life he wanted. In more traditional talk therapy, it would be very rare to intentionally locate the client's deepest wound during their first session. The client and the therapist would need to build up a considerable rapport before going I believe in going their straight away as long as the client feels they have some agency over the journey. Ryan, my job for Ryan is to protect him. Marissa and I must protect him from Ryan. I must protect him from loneliness.
