In my 30 years of practice, almost all of my diverse array of clients' problems stem from a very similar set of issues. In fact, through much observation and study, I've come to believe that all my clients generally fall into one of three categories. All clients have a presenting problem. As mentioned before, Ryan had several. He was struggling with addiction, low self-esteem, bad relationships, anxiety and depression, and more. But what lies beneath any client's presenting problem will always be something more fundamental, and it usually connects to one of the following three beliefs. The first belief is that you are not enough. It's the issue that's at the core of so many people's problems. Often it's just a matter of peeling back the layers of the client's issue, whether that is an addiction, workaholism, depression, over-eating, or accumulating possessions, and locating the point in time where they internalize the belief that they weren't enough. The rest of those issues are just manifestations of that hugely damaging belief. Children have one need to fulfill in their childhood to seek and receive the approval and love of their parents or caretakers. When they don't achieve that, it's so traumatic and disorienting that they can't rationalize it. It's impossible for a child to understand that while their parent is flawed, they are lovable despite their parents' inability to love them. So they internalize the belief that if their parent, the one person who is supposed to love them no matter what, doesn't love them, they must not be lovable at all. They are not enough. Even if parents do love a child, then someone else such as a sibling, relative, caregiver, or teacher can also instill in children the belief that they are not enough. This belief will follow them into adulthood, which is why I see grown-ups who report a lifetime of damage inflicted upon their self-esteem by a school bully who was able to make the child and then the adult they grew into feel that they would never ever be enough. Once you internalize that belief, it's very hard to even know it's affecting you because it's so fundamental and deeply held. It puts a filter on everything you do. That's exacerbated by the fact that society reinforces it in so many ways, from consumerism and unrealistic beauty standards to racism and a lack of tolerance for different beliefs. We'll develop all kinds of coping mechanisms to deal with this deeply uncomfortable belief, including addiction, compulsion, depression, and anxiety. In my therapist's chair, I've seen them all. However, I have watched over and over how a simple, profound, and life-changing mantra can replace this ultimate limiting belief and set you free. That mantra is, I am enough. This is a mantra you will hear throughout this book. The second fundamental belief that really damages people's lives is that they want something that's unavailable to them. So many clients come to me with a desperate longing to be free of their issues, but alongside the issues which can include depression, alcoholism, obesity, and lack of success is a fixed belief. This belief can come in many different packages. I want to be free of depression, but I have the depressed gene just like my mum. I want a successful relationship, but love is not available to me. Or maybe it's, I'm desperate to stop drinking, but I come from a family of alcoholics. Another common one is, I want to acquire wealth, but I don't have a college degree or the right background. I want to be confident, but I was born shy. The fixed beliefs my clients hold about themselves are the biggest blocks to achieving their goals. You know doubt have some fixed beliefs too, and it's very useful to ask yourself why you believe that. Where did that belief come from? Who gave it to you? Who gave it to them? Why are you still believing it all these years later? The minute you begin to question a belief, you no longer hold it to be true. You begin to chip away at it and diminish it. Once that belief has receded in its strength, it's time to replace it with a new one. Remember, many people who have dazzling success were not born into a position where it was made available to them. Oprah Winfrey, Barack Obama and Tony Robbins all found success, it did not find them. Successful people like this learn along the way that everything is available to them. The first step to achieving that is to fix that new belief firmly in your mind in place of the old one. The third problem that so many of my clients present with is a powerful belief they are different. This was the fundamental problem I identified early on with Ryan. The stories he brought up about his childhood while in hypnosis spoke to this belief. Being stuck in the changing room feeling awkward, being caught touching himself by the babysitter, being ignored of form of lack of connection in the classroom, and finally, and most fundamentally, being rejected by his father because he was gay. Over and over in life, the belief that he was different and therefore couldn't connect or be loved by others was reinforced. That feeling became so painful that he had to resort to substances to blunt the pain it caused. You can see how this looping thought works. The common denominator of all our emotional issues is that we feel we are not enough and we feel different so we can't connect. Yet our survival is linked to our need to connect, so it becomes a spiral, a vicious circle. Ryan's belief that he was different, unlovable and not able to connect was really rooted in his father's rejection of him at a very young age. He saw that belief reinforced in many areas of his life when he was growing up, which is why he brought up those specific stories first during our root cause work. We were able to replace his belief that he couldn't connect with the better, more compassionate story that his father was unable to connect with him. That news story is where lasting change comes from. Ryan's progress. Nearly three years after his session, Ryan describes himself as still sober, having far more confidence than he once had and no longer suffering from depression. Even though he was well into his forties when he met me, he reports that he spent most of his life having no idea that his negative self-talk and story about himself as being unlovable was the cause of all these issues in his life. I know now that I can control my feelings with my thoughts, he says. I didn't know how to do that before, and it's really a matter of the beliefs that I have. The beliefs are just thoughts that are repeated over and over again. He says RTT helped him replace the story that had been fueling his negative dialogue for years with a new, true one. The whole identity of being a monster for being a gay person. That was what society was putting onto me. It had nothing to do with me, Ryan says. When I say society, I mean people in my town. My own parents, everybody around me. It was their own belief that because somebody is gay they're an evil person. I just accepted that to be true. But now I can rationally see that's completely bullshit and wrong, and it never was true. Ryan says not only can he reject that belief outright now, he feels deeply proud of himself for surviving a childhood where he was infused with such harmful beliefs. I actually have more respect for myself for surviving and for figuring this out, Ryan says. It wasn't easy to figure all this out either about myself, and it took 47 years. I had no clue that anything was wrong. It really didn't occur to me. It just felt like I was a sad, depressed alcoholic with no future, and that was just who I was. I didn't really have the tools to do any sort of self-examination, and so I appreciate Marissa because she's the one who gave me the tools. Beautifully, Ryan now works with groups of people who are recovering from addiction, and he reports using some of the tools he learned in his RTT training to do so. The biggest takeaway of the session is that everything is really based on what we pick up in childhood. I use that often in my groups, Ryan says. You might have this weird belief that you're stupid or ugly, and that might have come from some little girl or boy on the playground who said that to you. Something reinforced it, and the belief just never went away. It's always there, and it's never disputed. So finding what it is, and then disputing it, is really key. So while it's clear he's far from the sad, depressed alcoholic he once was, how does Ryan describe himself today? I would describe myself as much more confident, much more at peace with who I am. I love who I am actually, I'm not perfect. I still have things to work on, but I know how to do that now. RTT for me, installing the cheerleader. Harsh, hurtful, critical words we say to ourselves over and over in our inner dialogue, can do severe damage over time. Many people like Ryan don't even realize they're doing it. They can go decades in life thinking that their inner voice is just expressing the so-called facts. You're stupid, you're dumb, nobody likes you. Over time this script becomes feelings and beliefs. They seem like the objective truth when in reality they were unhelpfully installed somewhere along the way. In order to change your inner dialogue, you first have to notice it's there. So do an inventory of what your inner voice is saying to you. If your outwardly depressed, sad or anxious, it's likely that your inner voice isn't very positive or helpful, and is adding to your suffering. Take note of the statements that come up over and over, perhaps jotting some of them down to keep track of them. Just noticing that this voice is not you, that there is a difference between your inherent essence and value and your inner monologue, can be the beginning of change. Many people live their whole lives without realising that. If you notice all the words you say to yourself are harsh and critical as Ryan did, it's time to stage something of an intervention. You can start with a technique I call installing the cheerleader. Imagine a cheerleader or other enthusiastic figure taking residence in your head. It only knows how to say positive and encouraging messages to you, and enjoys doing so repeatedly. Hear it in opposition to your critical voice, shouting and cheering you on. You can do this. Everyone wants you to succeed. You excel at everything you try. I'm rooting for you. You're amazing and kind and smart. If this sounds utterly ridiculous or silly to you, that's part of the point. Depersonalising this voice, making it into a kind of cartoonish figure, is a helpful way of letting it in. If you've been speaking to yourself in a harsh way for decades, your mind is going to struggle to immediately switch your inner voice over to a healthier, positive script. However, if you imagine this positive voice as someone other than you, even someone who's a little silly, it's easier to allow it in. Write down some lines you need to hear that this cheerleader may say to you, and put the list somewhere you'll see it often. You can also sit in front of the mirror for a few minutes each day and say the cheerleader's lines out loud. It doesn't matter how you do it, but repetition is key here. You need to reach a point where you begin to hear the cheerleader's voice in your head, yelling in opposition to your negative self-talk. Eventually, the hope here is that both your harsh critical voice and your loud, enthusiastic cheerleader can be replaced by a single, much more benevolent one. Your own voice, but the over-the-top cheerleader is the first step. Install it today and watch your inner dialogue change.

CHAPTER III. JEMMA It's easy to understand why people who have extreme issues or problems seek out transformation through therapy. When you are an addict, are destructive to yourself and others, or have a repetitive habit that is hugely interfering with your life. It is often a practical matter that brings you into the therapy chair. Life simply can't go on like this anymore. We have all kinds of language for this in popular culture, including hitting rock bottom, or reaching a do or die, or now or never moment. While it's true that some people decide to change when they reach their lowest point, it can also be somewhat of a disheartening message. After all, where does that leave the rest of us? Do our lives have to become so dark, dour and desperate before we can choose to transform? I believe the answer to that is no, and I love JEMMA's story because it proves that is just not the case. JEMMA's presenting problems were not what I would classify as severe or extreme in any way. Mostly she said she just wanted to feel less sad. In addition, she reported a lack of confidence as well as depression, anxiety and problems with her weight. I'm sure anyone who met JEMMA or knew her casually would not think of her as a person with tremendous troubles. As such, it was easy to imagine her going through her entire life feeling sad. She probably would have survived that way, but her life certainly wouldn't have reached its richest potential. It can feel daunting as a therapist when someone presents with multiple problems that are affecting their life in a low-grade way. It's hard to know where to start. In response to that complexity, it's tempting to buy into this idea that we need to spend weeks, months or years of talk therapy to figure out what is at the source of their many problems. But weeks, months or years of therapy also means weeks, months or years of a client being sad or suffering. RTT stands a part because of my belief that we can identify the core of someone suffering, even if it's not acute or extreme, by taking a much more direct route. JEMMA is a highly educated scientist with a PhD in biochemistry. She is rational and scientific and has a great mind, which is really a therapist's dream, because she is so inquisitive and articulate with a rich self-knowledge. During the intake when I asked JEMMA where her sadness came from, she mentioned losing her mother to cancer several years ago. She explained that she had actually been motivated to go into her field of study, which was cancer research, because her family had been personally touched by the disease. Her mother was first diagnosed with breast cancer in 2000, right around the time JEMMA embarked on her studies. There are few things as taxing and challenging as completing a PhD program, so to devote all that energy to a cause related to her mother's sickness is interesting to me. It makes me wonder if she felt a responsibility to save her mother, one that still haunted her. Before we entered a hypnosis state, I asked her if she felt any guilt for failing to keep her mother from dying of cancer. Unsurprisingly, she became emotional, indicating that guilt was perhaps beneath her sadness. While I don't delight in seeing a client upset, it's always something of a gift when a client gets emotional so early into a session. Especially in the intake process. When I bring up a topic and I see a client's chin wobble, their eyes get teary or their voice crack, I take note of what they've responded to. I don't necessarily press them on it right away, but I know that I found something that can serve as an opening. In this case, I knew we needed to explore JEMMA's guilt. I was struck by the fact that the thing JEMMA reported she wanted to fix the most was her sadness. sadness is such an interesting emotion, especially when it stays with us for a long, long time. It's appropriate to be sad when bad things happen or we experience a loss, and we should allow ourselves to feel that fully when it happens. But when a person feels sad over many years in a low grade yet stubborn way, the sadness can be masking something else. Perhaps for JEMMA, sadness was an accessible emotion that had become normalized and accepted in her life. It was possible that sadness was masking some other feelings that weren't so easy for her to feel and express. This was something I also made a note to explore. Another thing that I noticed during our short intake was what JEMMA said about her husband. She used the language that she follows him around the world for his job, and blindly said his career and qualifications were much more impressive than her own, even though they met doing the same studies. When I asked her if she liked that dynamic, she said yes, but I found her word choice in drinking. In describing her role in her own marriage, she was describing a person with little agency. JEMMA's session. When I finally began hypnosis and root cause work with JEMMA, it did not take long for her to identify the scenes at the source of her sadness and depression. I think it's a testament to the power of hypnosis that someone with a rather vague sense of their sadness when they are in a normal, awakened state goes to very precise and detailed memories from many years ago, just a few minutes later. The first memory that came up very quickly was as a small child of two. She was trying to climb over a baby gate so she could reach her mum. She said, I need my mum but I can't have her, and that makes me feel sad. It also makes me feel alone. She went on, I want to be in her arms, I need to be in her arms. But I can't get into her arms, and now I feel angry with my dad because she would let me, and he won't. She spoke with great desperation and sadness. Immediately JEMMA's sadness went straight to the source feeling, anger, specifically anger with her dad. While years and years of history and hurt and sadness stood before the JEMMA of today and the two-year-old JEMMA, that feeling was still there, still so accessible to her. It was just lying under the surface. We live in a culture where we are taught that life is dominated by facts, and logic, and absolutes. On the surface it can certainly seem that way, but that's not really what drives and motivates humans at their core. I believe that feelings not facts are the most real thing we have, and as a therapist you don't really want the client to be logical. You want to get them to feel the feelings as much and as quickly as possible. It can be difficult to revisit these things when they involve pain and sadness as JEMMA's story clearly did, but she did so beautifully and quickly as we began our root cause work. She knew exactly where to go. She knew that little girl of two felt sad, lost and helpless, but mostly she felt powerless because she couldn't get over that gate. She also recalled hearing her mother crying and having the sense that her mother wanted to let her in the room but could not. The precise facts of this memory did her father actually stop her, was her mother really crying because she couldn't reach her. There's some what immaterial here. Whether she was remembering accurately or not, she had the feeling that she wanted to get to her mother and her mother wanted her, but she couldn't fix it. That feeling was supremely real to JEMMA right up to the day we met. It's worth remembering here what JEMMA presented with before we started root cause work in hypnosis. She'd lost her mum and she felt tremendous guilt about it. But she felt in her forties was precisely what she felt when she was a toddler. In a similar scene, JEMMA remembered being told to stay in her bed because there was a new baby, her younger sibling. Her father told her to get back to her room and stay in her room. Again, she pined for her mother. Again, her father stood in the way. Again, she felt helpless and forgotten, and now with a new baby on the scene, she felt like she was second best. It was clear to me at this stage that JEMMA was an adult woman who was acting with the unmet needs of a child. As we learned in Carrie's story, children have quite fundamental needs regardless of their culture or background. They need to feel safe and loved. They need to feel they matter. JEMMA didn't appear to experience any abuse or mistreatment, but she still had this deep memory of an unmet need. And when a child's fundamental needs are not met, they often go through life with these beliefs, which take on an adult dimension. No one is going to love me. I am never safe. I have to look for someone else to make me feel that I'm important and I matter. People with unmet childhood needs often try to give someone else a lover, partner or even their own child their needs to take care of. They desperately hope that this person can finally meet those needs after so long. As I pressed JEMMA on how the new baby's arrival made her feel, she said something that peaked my interest. I feel second best and I don't like this baby because it's taken my attention. It was a dynamic that sounded quite similar to how she described her marriage. Her husband had the impressive job title. Despite the fact they met at the same university and studied the same topic. He was the one who dictated where the family lived. JEMMA was just a supporting act, much like she felt with her younger sibling. JEMMA is a perfect example of a client who had feelings that were exactly the same as they were during an early childhood event. The veracity or particulars of these events don't really matter. The feelings do. She hadn't been able to accept losing her mamas and adult because the feelings of losing her mum to a sibling as a young child were never dealt with. As an extension of that, she settled for feeling second best to her husband because that was the feeling that became familiar when her younger sibling came along. You may think plenty of people have younger siblings who come along and it doesn't haunt them for the rest of their adult lives. And that's true. However, it's not the event that affects you, it's the meaning of the event, the interpretation. It was clear to me that in JEMMA's mind the belief was, I've been replaced. Someone better has come along and now I'm not enough. I need to stay close to my mum at all costs. JEMMA had bought into that belief and kept it with her her entire life. This point bears emphasizing and repeating because it is so important to RTT and to understanding human behaviour in general. The significance of an event is dictated by how you feel about it. The things that run and often ruin people's lives are not objective versions of reality, but faulty or unhelpful interpretations of events. Terrible things can happen to people, but if they are in a healthy supportive environment where they are able to process and honour their feelings in real time with adequate support, they are less likely to adopt a belief system that, for example, causes them to blame themselves or feel that they are unlovable. This is what this whole book and RTT itself is about, telling yourself a better lie. We usually cannot change the events or bad things that happen to us, especially as children, and we can change the stories we tell ourselves about those events. Of course it would be ideal if we were all born to perfect parents who know exactly how to love us and meet our emotional needs, but that is just not the case. However, we don't need to walk around our entire lives with the belief that our father left, our mum ignored us, or our younger sibling was loved more than us because of some deficiency or defect in ourselves. Chapter 5. Joe I first gained a reputation as a rule-breaking therapist through my work with weight loss clients. This was something of an accident. While I was working in Los Angeles as a fitness instructor, I noticed that virtually every other person who came to my class was struggling with food in some way. They had overly restrictive diets or were compulsively exercising, despite the fact that they were the picture of health on the outside. It was my first clue that our persistent issues with food and weight, whether they stem from not eating enough or eating far too much, have little to do with food at all. They are a stand-in for something else entirely. Later on, I worked with people on the other end of the weight spectrum, including on TV programmes like Celebrity Fit Club and Super Size vs Super Skinny. On those shows, I met overweight celebrities and people who is entire livelihoods and futures depended on them losing weight. They had every reason, motivation and resource at their disposal to do it, yet they hadn't been able to. That's because before they met me, they'd been treating their weight problem as a physical one. But like anything else we treat using RTT, eating too much or too little is merely a behaviour that's serving a purpose. Don't treat the behaviour, find the reason behind it and the purpose it's serving. Indeed, it's no secret that weight is such a vexing issue in our society and culture. But it was in those days in Los Angeles that I started to view it quite differently from others. The struggle to lose weight is often framed as a problem that comes from a lack of knowledge. In other words, all you have to do to fix the problem is inform someone what to eat and when and how much to exercise, and they will no longer find themselves unable to lose weight and keep it off. Of course, if this were true then the entire diet and weight loss industry wouldn't exist, and people wouldn't spend their entire lives switching from diet to diet, trying to lose weight and sometimes succeeding only to gain it all back again. The truth is, when it comes to the diet and exercise equation, most people do not have a knowledge gap. They already know what they should be doing. We all do. It's ingrained into us from such a young age. Few people actually believe that eating junk food can't eat chips and fast food take out day after day is good for them. Indeed, there is little disagreement as to what constitutes a healthy diet over the long term. We can look at years and years of research and common sense and plainly see that diets are high in lean protein, healthy fats and plants and low in refined carbs and sugars. Essentially the food humans ate before processed food was so accessible, promote optimal health. If you tell a person who has struggled with a weight problem their entire life to simply eat less and exercise more, they will roll their eyes at you. They've undoubtedly heard this advice a million times. They've probably even tried it, but it's so often just doesn't work over the long term. So if it's not a knowledge gap, what is it? Of course, there are some structural and societal problems that contribute such as inadequate access to healthy, affordable food, that is common for low income people living in rich countries. I don't want to diminish factors such as that as they do play a role in the high obesity rates we see in countries like the US and the UK. However, when it comes to the level of the individual and the people I usually see in my office, issues with weight very often have at their core an emotional truth or fixed belief. This is especially true when someone has struggled with weight their entire life or from a young age. Joe was a perfect example of this. She came to me with the desire to take control of her weight which she reported she had struggled with since her 20s, if not earlier. In many ways Joe's story is unremarkable and familiar to many. She was now in her mid-50s still struggling with her weight and still finding herself powerless when it came to resisting the food she knew weren't good for her, such as chocolate, cookies and cola. Her weight wasn't so severe that it was life threatening, but it was undoubtedly holding back her life to a significant degree. Having recently learned that she was pre-diabetic, she rightly wanted to reverse the course of type 2 diabetes while she still could. On a deep level, I sensed that she recognized that when it came to her weight loss and taking control of her body, it was now or never. I asked Joe how she felt in her body, how it felt physically to walk around in her shoes. This can be a very revealing question. After all, a number on a scale can give us some measure of information and may be useful to a doctor, but it doesn't tell the whole picture. Often how a person feels in their body can be much more telling than their medical charts. As I learned in those fitness classes all those years ago, even people who appear to be extremely healthy and eat diets that dieticians would approve of can be at silent war with their bodies. An answer to that question, Joe reported that she feels heavy and unable to control my own movements, as if she was carrying something around that wasn't even hers. She struggled to get around most days and found physical existence to be something of a burden. The excess weight she had didn't feel like it should be there, like it was a stand-in for something else. In addition, Joe reported a kind of listless feeling about her life. She worked in a job that didn't feel meaningful and often found herself wondering what the point of life was at all. She wanted to find a loving partner but felt far from being able to do that. Having recently suffered a foot injury as well, she said she easily got in a self-perpetuating cycle of defeat wherein she couldn't do the walking exercise she wanted because of her foot and thus she felt unmotivated to try to sort out her weight problem because she couldn't exercise. It felt as though everything she wanted wasn't hers to have. Joe was a smart, accomplished and well-traveled 56-year-old woman who knew exactly how to lose weight, like most of us do. But that knowledge had not translated into the outcome she desired. There had to be a reason for that, likely unrelated to food, her affinity for chocolate or her willingness to exercise. If it were that simple, she undoubtedly would have solved this problem ages ago. She was like so many other people who struggled with weight. They believe they are facing a dietary problem, but in fact they are facing an emotional one. We used RTT to figure out what that problem was. Joe's session It was interesting that in Joe's intake session we didn't speak much about her childhood or family history. Often that can be helpful in the intake, but it can also be revealing to leave it for once we're in hypnosis. CHAPTER VI. LUCY Depression and suicide are some of the great tragedies of the modern world. Despite all the technological and social progress that humanity has made over centuries, the issue of depression is one that we have not only not learned how to solve, but has actually got worse. The problem seems to be worse in developed countries like the US and the UK, where depression and suicide are an epidemic. The World Health Organization states that depression is a leading cause of disability worldwide and is a major contributor to the overall global burden of disease. So how can a problem simultaneously be so intractable and so widespread? Clearly, the way we are thinking about and treating this problem is not serving the millions, if not billions, of people who suffer from it. If it were, more and more people wouldn't be struggling with these modern ailments year after year. LUCY was one of those people in a state of deep pain and suffering. When I asked her the desired outcome of our session, her hope was as simple as it was sad. She hoped to be able to resist the urge to take her own life, something that she had attempted three times already. LUCY was now 41 and she said her depression had been with her for a long time. She had been on medication countless times, frustrated by doctors who insisted that this was the only way for her to feel better. She had tried talk therapy, which she said was sometimes helpful, but more often left her feeling frustrated by therapists who kept asking her how she felt, the answer, terrible. And the deep love for her children and a devotion to her Christian faith, LUCY desperately wanted to live. She wanted to want to live to be more precise. She was ashamed that she had had these thoughts of wanting to kill herself and didn't understand why she couldn't get rid of them. Before we went into hypnosis or began to recall any scenes, LUCY volunteered some information. She said, every time I hear the word womb, I think about how my mum told me she cried for the first six months while she was pregnant with me. She didn't think she could cope with me. So I suppose I think if you didn't want me, why should I be here? The answer to that question was that a force bigger than LUCY's mother wanted her to be here. This force is present in all of us, a literal life force that is our strongest, most elemental instinct. It helps us to stay alive even in situations where we are convinced we shouldn't be. It's why so many people who survive an unsuccessful suicide attempt reveal that seconds after pulling the trigger or jumping off a structure, they wish they hadn't done it. While we can think of this force as a purely evolutionary trait, we can also see it as a spiritual one too. It was that life force, that belief in her own worthiness that we needed to reactivate in LUCY. She already had it. She had just forgotten how to hear it. In my experience, I have found that there are generally three broad reasons people experience depression and by extension, a desire to not be alive. The first is not following a person's heart or desire. Countless times I've met with clients who dreamed of being an actor or musician in their lives but for whatever reason ended up doing something else. While their lives may look more than adequate on the surface, they have a strong conviction inside of them that they were meant to do something else. Until they heed that it's difficult for them to feel like they are fulfilling their lives or ever will. While having a strong calling and denying it is one manifestation of this cause, it can be more prosaic than that too. Too many people in the modern world have jobs where they don't feel like they have any agency or make any impact on their community or the people around them. These kinds of jobs where people spend their time day in day out without any real tangible outcome for their efforts can certainly cause depression too. We can't spend the majority of our lives doing things that don't bring any satisfaction or meaning and expect to not pay a price. Of course, this doesn't mean everyone has to become an actor or musician. Indeed being a hairdresser, builder or driver can bring great satisfaction if workers are treated well and feel like they have a connection to the people and community they serve or work for. That connection or lack thereof is related to the second cause of depression. Feeling disconnected, the second cause of depression I often observe can come in many forms. We know from the three things wrong with everybody which we covered in chapter 1 that a feeling of disconnection can stem from childhood bullying, parents who rejected you or any number of traumatic early scenes. But it can also be exacerbated by a modern lifestyle where more and more people live alone rather than in the tribal or community-based structures we evolve to live in. Add to that our obsession with living life through our screens rather than relating to one another and you can see how this problem has become so widespread. Lack of connection is sadly one of the defining features of our modern era. The third reason people experience depression is harsh, hurtful, critical words that they say to themselves on a daily basis. These words very often stem from an early belief that a person is not enough. But they are once again exacerbated by a culture that encourages us to look a certain way, act a certain way and have certain material goods in order to be accepted. If we already believe we're not enough from a very young age, it can be nearly impossible to counter the unending messages from society that reinforce that flawed belief. Notice how none of the reasons I just listed include a chemical imbalance or one's genetic or biological makeup. Yet that is the primary story people are told when they seek treatment for depression from conventional medicine. In other words, something is wrong with your brain chemistry. Here is a pill to fix it. Lucy experienced that when she went to a doctor for yet another spell of depression and suicidal thoughts and he told her, you've had three spells of this, you're clinically depressed and you have to be on this medication for all your life. She reported deep down knowing that the medication was not her way out. It's controversial to challenge the conventional wisdom that psychological problems like depression can be solved with medication and I'm not saying that genetics and biology don't predispose a person to struggle with these ailments in some cases. Nor am I saying that medication doesn't help some people in certain acute situations. But I firmly believe that biology is not destiny. And for far too long the cultural script and dominant medical paradigm has been that depression is the result of a chemical imbalance and therefore only able to be treated with pills. This has happened though these medications don't always help a lot of people they're intended to, especially over the long term. As one study published in 2020 rather succinctly put it, currently there is no reliable evidence that long term antidepressant treatment is beneficial and there are legitimate concerns that it may be largely ineffective or even harmful in a substantial portion of users. In his book Lost Connections, author Johann Harry explains the alternative view that a matrix of biological, psychological and social factors cause issues like depression and anxiety, not merely genetic predisposition. This is known in research literature as the bio-psychosocial model and was pioneered in the 1970s by a physician named George Engel, who was critical of the narrow biomedical model that medicine in the West has followed since the 20th century. In summarizing the present day research, Harry explains that science has found evidence of nine different causes of depression and anxiety. Only two of them are related to our biology or genetics, the rest are factors in the way we live. In a TEDx talk related to his book, Harry tells a great story of a village in Cambodia when a South African psychiatrist went to study the effects of chemical antidepressants when they were first introduced there in the early 2000s. The local healers and doctors were perplexed at the idea of using chemical antidepressants, saying they already had a solution for this problem. The researchers wanted to know what that solution was. The local healers and doctors described a farmer whose leg had been blown off by a mine while he was working in the rice fields. After physically recovering and receiving an artificial limb, the man went back to work in those same fields. However, he found he was in a lot of pain from working underwater with a prosthesis and was also very depressed. People in the community came to speak to him and tried to understand the source of his pain and suffering, which included the fact that he had to spend every day at the scene of his trauma. It was plain to see why this situation was making him depressed. He was in physical pain and every day he had to return to the place that gave him that pain. So the community members got together and bought him a cow. When he no longer had to work in the rice fields because he could be a dairy farmer instead, the man's depression quickly lifted. The local doctors said to the researcher, so you see the cow is the antidepressant. That's what you mean, right? The Cambodians understood that this man who was so sad and depressed needed connection. He needed a daily purpose that didn't cause him pain. And above all, he needed to change the circumstances that were making him depressed. Too often in our culture, we revert straight to the chemical solution without addressing those things first. CHAPTER 7. Justin Modern Western medicine has made such stunning advances in our lifetime that you'd be a fool to want to be alive in any other era. Once upon a time illnesses or accidents we now consider minor or routine could have seriously threatened a person's life. However, while advances in the medical field are not to be under appreciated, they do not represent the full spectrum of where healing comes from. Generally speaking, Western medicine is based on the paradigm known as mind body dualism. This is the idea that the mind and body are separate entities and that physical ailments should be treated with targeted interventions such as drugs or surgery. It dates back to René Descartes of the 17th century who was pushing back against the religious norms of the day. His idea that the material body should be considered separate from the immaterial mind helped free up the body to be studied by the sciences, paving the way for great scientific and medical advancements. While it's a good thing science progresses to figure out how to treat illnesses using methods other than prayers and superstition, it seems we've gone a little too far in that direction. These days, the paradigm upon which all Western medicine and healthcare is built seems to discount the many ways that physical health intersects psychological, social, cultural and environmental issues. Modern medicine can be so narrowly focused on cause and effect that it fails to take a holistic picture of healing into account. In some corners of medicine, it's even considered controversial or lacking in evidence to suggest that what you eat and putting your body day after day can have a huge impact on whether you're able to heal from a disease or even whether you develop one to begin with. There is no shortage of healing traditions that long predate conventional Western medicine to suggest that is not the case. And intuitively, we know that our health is affected by things like our diet, our stress levels and our emotional health. Once a person becomes accustomed to being in a state of starvation, which happens shockingly quickly, their body and mind becomes adapted to that state and takes on a whole new way of surviving. One eating disorder specialist I worked with said that when a person's weight gets to 85% of what it should be for their height, their entire thought process shifts to one of starvation mode. They stop adhering to the rationality, decision making, and facts they would if they weighed a bit more. Starvation doesn't just create physical changes in the body, but psychological ones too. So when it comes to eating disorders, clinicians can find themselves in a bind. Real healing lies not in repairing the ties with the person who hurt us, but in repairing our relationship with ourselves. They believe making them revisit the specific memories of the horrible things that happen to them will reactivate all the pain and fear that they felt when the initial event happened. There's an idea that it's not necessary or worse that it may even set them back on their course of healing. The viewpoint that we should avoid resurfacing traumatic events also discounts the fact that many people are already living with their trauma as a visceral and present force in their lives. There is a proliferation of research that shows how trauma is not just a psychological experience but has physical manifestations too. When trauma lodges itself in the body and gets stuck, it can take all kinds of different forms from addiction and chronic pain to insomnia and skin problems. The list goes on because everyone's trauma can manifest differently. Renowned trauma researcher Bessel van der Kolk wrote a book about this emerging field and aptly titled it. The body keeps the score, brain, mind and body in the healing of trauma. I call it my upper limit, my chief fun inhibitor. It didn't matter what I did in my life. I found that there was a part of me that felt I didn't deserve to be happy. I couldn't just let go and have fun. It didn't matter what I did, where I went to live. I sold companies lived an incredible lifestyle, but it still wasn't quite enough. I just had that feeling that I didn't deserve to be happy, so I just felt overly responsible for other people, so there was my guilt. Daniel wanted help solving a phobia, but what he really needed to do was to locate and understand an unmet need. After doing that so well for himself, he now helps others do the same with RTT. RTT for me, becoming your own loving parent. Daniel had a memory of an adverse early life experience that went on to affect his entire life, from the very time he was brought home from the hospital. He had no idea that this event was affecting his life so much, and indeed many people are shaped by hazy events that happened to them long before they had any agency or power. Indeed, in some cases, these are events that happened before they could even walk or talk. We have two choices when faced with this somewhat dispiriting truth. We can sadly accept that our lives were messed up from day one by a misunderstanding or by things we couldn't control. Or we can take the power back and give something better back to our early selves. In RTT terms, the latter of these two approaches is a three-pronged method I've mentioned elsewhere in the book, such as in Carrie's chapter. Becoming a loving parent, upgrading the child and merging the child. When you become your own loving parent, you can forgive your own parents and caretakers for letting you down, because it's not their job anymore. It's your job to make sure your inner child is well taken care of. This is such a simple, elegant shift to make mentally. But as you will see throughout the stories in this book, it can change your entire life. You can be the person your inner child is waiting for. Upgrading the child is not about changing the reality of what happened to you in the past or pretending it doesn't exist. It's about imbuing a belief deep within you, where that inner child still lives today, that things are different now. It's reimagining that early experience and recasting it in your mind. It's a powerful visualization exercise that can prevent you from hanging on to early life events that you can't change or control. Finally, we merge that safe inner child with the person you are today. To do this exercise, find a comfortable seat or lie down. Make sure you're comfortable and warm and that you won't be disturbed by another person or a phone ringing. Guiding you through this meditation, I will ask you to imagine yourself through a similar scenario to Daniel. Going to claim the baby that was you and picking up the baby which is you. Take that baby home to a safe and loving place. Allow the powerful visualization to help you become a loving parent to yourself. CHAPTER 11. MY STORY When you have had a career as long and high profile as mine, you will always find there a naysayers or people who want to doubt your success. Honestly, that's fine with me. I have the immense gratification of hearing from and speaking with the many people who have been helped by my work and by RTD. And that's all the validation I need. However, there's a recurring misconception that often comes up from these doubters. They seem to think that if you take the tenets of RTT onboard and master the rules of your mind, nothing bad will ever happen to you. Using me as an example, they reason that if anything bad has ever happened to me, which of course it has because I'm human, it's proof that my methods don't work. I began to notice this when I went public with two cancer diagnosis and recoveries. These anonymous commenters would say, well, if RTT works so well why'd she get cancer? I'm not foolish enough to try to reason with anonymous internet commenters. Their pain is always evident in their anger. However, their misunderstanding offers a good lesson. It doesn't matter if we're talking about RTT, my life or yours. Bad, inconvenient heart-breaking things will happen. It's how you choose to face and bounce back from them that determines the trajectory of your life. I first started to learn this lesson as a young adult. A doctor told me that I would never be able to get pregnant and that if I did I wouldn't be able to carry a healthy child to term. As I was just embarking on adulthood, I wasn't even trying to get pregnant at the time, so it was quite a strangely alarmist diagnosis to give such a young woman. It was in that doctor's office. Perhaps for the first time, I heard a voice speak up with a very clear directive. Don't let that in. I could sense that it was not helpful to listen to this doctor give me this negative diagnosis at this stage in my life, especially because I wasn't yet trying to have a child. I decided to leave the doctor's office and not dwell too much on what he had said. Years later, when I did become pregnant with my daughter, doctors similarly told me the pregnancy likely wouldn't be a successful one. They said even if I did manage to give birth at full term, my daughter would likely be underweight. They advised me not to even try. Again, I decided not to let that in and gave birth to my daughter, Phaedra, at a healthy 7.8 pounds nine months later. None of this is to say you shouldn't listen to doctors or seek their care, but rather be careful about letting in what they're telling you because it doesn't have to be your destiny. I learned this lesson again in 2015 when I was diagnosed with womb cancer. For the first day or so, I felt shocked and devastated in quick succession. To be totally honest, I couldn't believe this had happened to me. One thing I'll never forget is when I asked the doctor if after surgery, the cancer would come back and he knocked his fist on the table and said, the cancer has your address. It knows where you live, so even if we remove it with surgery, it will probably come back. Again, I thought, wow, I cannot let this in. This is such a strange thing to hear. I was advised that the best course of medical action was to schedule a hysterectomy. Of course, this was a big surgery and it had to be performed quickly. I decided that other than entrusting the skilled doctors to ably perform my surgery, the rest of my treatment and recovery had to be up to me. After all, I had lots going on in my life at that point. I was just about to launch my new RTT training school and I had speaking engagements and travel commitments in just a week's time. So I began to tell myself, this is just a blip. I will go for the surgery. It will work and my body will recover swiftly and fully. Doctors advised me that I had to be in the hospital for days after the surgery. I would be on bed rest and travel was out of the question any time in the near future. Respectfully, I told them that while I entrusted them to perform the surgery to their highest capabilities, the recovery process would be under my control. I ended up staying in the hospital for just one night. A week later, I was on stage speaking. And three weeks later, I flew to fulfill my professional commitment in Costa Rica. I knew that what would make me happy and helped me heal fastest, was not lying in bed and thinking, oh, I'm so ill. I've had major surgery and all I can do is lie here. I may have had cancer, but I wasn't going to let that take over my entire life. After all, I had so much to live for. My doctors and nurses were amazed at how swift my recovery was and even asked me how I'd managed to do it so they could inform other patients it was possible to get back to health so quickly. One of the main things I did was create a new narrative in my mind. Instead of telling myself I was so unlucky for getting cancer, I talked to my body and mind and said, this is actually great. I don't need a womb because I've already had my child. I'm so lucky. It could have been an eye, a leg, or a bone, but it's an organ I don't need, what a stroke of luck. I also used command cell therapy, which is an RTT technique I've mentioned elsewhere in this book. Using precise, direct, and evocative language, you literally command your body to get better. You don't want to say, I want my body to get better. No. You say, I direct, command, insist, and instruct it to get better. I imagined my womb surrounded by robust fighting cells. It was very important that the cancer didn't go from my womb to another organ, so I imagined a little fortress around it, with natural killer T cells fighting off the cancer. These cells recognized foreign invaders like viruses and tumors and killed them off. I was constantly commanding the body to do what it was meant to do, which is to work perfectly using its innate intelligence. Another thing I did was ensure that the treatment and surgery process itself was not filled with day after day of trauma and stress. So, for example, when I was going for a scan in a claustrophobic machine, I would hypnotize myself to imagine I was cozy and snuggled in my bed totally chilled, rather than rigid and scared of the result of the scan. Using this healing vortex technique on myself, I kept my body in a state of relaxation and ease rather than tension and hypervigilance, with stress hormones coursing through me causing more inflammation. The healing vortex can provide this place of rest and healing, even in moments when we might otherwise be stressed. Many people find this state of hypnosis, which can be reached with an audio recording or live hypnosis, immensely relaxing and healing. You are what you think. I know for some people it seems controversial to say that taking control of your thoughts and thinking positively affects your healing from something as serious as cancer, but it really shouldn't be. Every day there's proof that our thoughts create physical outcomes. If you imagine holding a lemon up to your mouth and taking a big bite out of it, your lips will pucker and your mouth will start to salivate. If you think an uncomfortable or embarrassing thought, you blush. If you think a sad thought, your eyes fill up with tears. If you think a sexual thought, you feel aroused. We know that thoughts have an immediate physical effect on the body because we experience it in a mundane sense every day. Furthermore, the entire field of sport psychology is proof that mind-based interventions such as visualization, negative thought stopping, positive goal setting, and relaxation paired with concentration have a real effect on physical outcomes. The famous golfer Arnold Palmer is famous for saying that 90% of the game is psychological, with just 10% physical. We don't find it hard to believe that if a swimmer imagines themselves swimming faster than they ever have before, and doesn't allow any thought to the contrary to take hold in their head, then the result will be an enhanced performance, and in fact studies have proven this is the case. So why can't we also believe the same about our body's capacity to help heal itself? Our bodies do what our minds repeatedly tell them to. I believe that's as true for a swimmer or a runner as it is for a patient. There's a lot of scientific proof of this happening in a medical context too. The placebo effect wherein people who think they are receiving a medical treatment see a positive outcome even though they have received a sugar pill is well documented. It accounts for anywhere between 15 percent and a whopping 72 percent of cure rates. This means when we use our minds to create the expectation we are going to heal. In other words, taking a sugar pill when we're told it's real medicine, our bodies can sometimes outperform an actual medication. It's our bodies meeting our minds expectations. The placebo effect is especially effective for chronic stress and inflammation conditions, pain management, depression, and the side effects of chemotherapy and cancer treatment. As a fascinating 2018 article in The New York Times about the emerging science around the placebo effect put it, tell someone a normal milkshake is a diet beverage and his gut will respond as if the drink willow fat. Take athletes to the top of the Alps, put them on exercise machines and hook them to an oxygen tank and they will perform better than when they are breathing room air. Even if room air is all that's in the tank. Wake a patient from surgery and tell him you've done an arthroscopic repair and his knee gets better even if all you did was knock him out and put a couple of incisions in his skin. Give a drug a fancy name and it works better than if you don't. In other words, the article goes on to say, the placebo is a powerful medical treatment that is ignored by doctors only at their patients' expense. In fact, studies are showing that the placebo effect is getting stronger each year and drug companies are scrambling to figure out why the human body is doing an increasingly good job of healing itself without the help of their drugs. The opposite of this is also true, giving us the no-sebo effect. This occurs when a person's expectation of pain or a negative outcome in the body actually causes the body to create symptoms. For example, a 2017 study in the European Journal of Pain followed 104 patients who had back surgery. When it came to pain after surgery, the researchers found that the patients who had a high level of anxiety and hypervigilance about post-surgery pain were in fact the ones who experienced the most pain. The researchers thought this expectation of pain was even more powerful than pain resulting from actual tissue damage or inflammation. While it's fair to say that thinking positively doesn't work for everybody all the time and may not give you the exact outcome you want without fail, it is absolutely based in science to say it can promote positive physical outcomes and enhance the effectiveness of your treatment. In fact, the placebo effect is so powerful that every single drug trial has to account for it. In other words, drug makers have to prove their drug is more effective than a placebo, not just the absence of treatment. If our minds are so powerful that they can turn a sugar pill into an effective treatment, why would anyone not take advantage of that power within? It's free and science-based and most importantly, it works and unlike medication, it does not have side effects. After the first cancer recovery, life moved on and for a while I thought cancer and I were done and then in 2017 I was diagnosed again this time with a different cancer. Once again I found this very difficult, perhaps even more difficult than the first time because unlike my womb, this organ couldn't be removed as easily. In fact I opted to forgo the surgery to fully remove it for various reasons. I worried that perhaps I'd become too blase and assumed cancer wouldn't come back again. However, despite my own doubts and the people who had doubted me after my first cancer experience, I returned to what I knew to be true. I had too much to live for and I was not going anywhere. This second operation and its recovery was admittedly more difficult than the first time around and while I didn't get back to normal quite as quickly as I'd planned, I still knew that I had to decide how to feel. So again, I used command cell therapy and hypnosis during my recovery because I had to live on a very limited diet of essentially just water, vegetables and fish. I hypnotized myself not to desire coffee, snacks or anything that would stand in the way of my healing. By hypnotizing myself to have this very powerful state of mind, I bounced back to where I was before and after having the surgery in September 2017, I was back teaching RTT in London in late October and in LA teaching my RTT course in November. Finding a purpose. Throughout both the cancer diagnoses, the knowledge that I had an RTT school to lead kept me going. In the moments when I wondered how I was going to get out of bed and find the strength to teach, I remembered that I simply had to because there was so much I still intended to accomplish. I believe that aspect of my healing was very important. I had a purpose. I had a reason. I had a determination and I was doing what I really loved which really helped. Looking back at my life, I realized that I learned this lesson as a child watching my parents who had two very different approaches to life. My father was a head teacher and he deeply loved his job, determinedly leaving the house for school every day with his briefcase under his arm. He experienced cancer twice in his life but you'd scarcely have noticed it. It was simply not on his agenda to dwell on his sickness and I don't think he ever took a day off work. My mother, on the other hand, was always sick and her bedroom contained so many medications it looked like a pharmacy. She was always rushing off to the doctors concerned about this or that. Knowing what I know now, I think the role function and purpose of her constant illnesses was to make her feel important. The doctors and nurses and endless diagnoses gave her care and attention she wasn't getting elsewhere. In keeping with the cultural norm at the time, she did not have a career or job outside the home. While some women find raising children is plenty to keep them fulfilled, I don't think she was one of those women and I think her life really suffered for it. My father, without either of us realizing it at the time, served as my greatest teacher. He showed me that having a purpose that fulfills you in life helps blunt the pain and give you strength when hardships come up. That's something those critics I mentioned earlier don't seem to understand. It's not if life goes wrong or a rye, it's when. No one gets to live a perfect life, but we all get the gift of deciding how to respond to what comes up, including sickness and serious illness like cancer. Would I have preferred not to get cancer twice? Of course I would have. Would I prefer to live in a world where I could ward off all inconvenience trauma, sadness, bad luck and misfortune? You bet. But as the subjects of this book have shown, the triumph is not in preventing anything bad from ever happening to you. It is in overcoming it when it does. It is in not allowing your childhood, diagnosis, history, or abuse to be the thing that defines the course of your entire life. It is about choosing a better story to tell yourself, and in my case, it was that I was not a person unlucky enough to get cancer twice, but rather a person who was lucky enough to overcome it twice. I also want to say, in case this isn't already abundantly clear, that healing ourselves thoroughly is not an either or in-devour. When you're ill, it's advisable to look at every avenue for healing. If you have a heart problem, you change your diet and do gentle exercise, as well as exploring surgery with a cardiac specialist. If you have a bad back, you take some medication and go to see a chiropractor. RTT is never offered in place of medical treatment, but as a powerful enhancement of it, as we saw with Justin's story. I want to say emphatically here, I'm not suggesting that RTT cures cancer. However, since the cancer diagnoses and recoveries, I've worked with many people with cancer, and often we use RTT to help chemotherapy patients to get their body to react to and recover from it better. We also use it to help people recover from surgeries faster and more completely. Throughout my career, I've helped many women successfully complete rounds of IVF, resulting in gorgeous, healthy babies, when numerous previous attempts have failed. In all these cases, these people are receiving medical treatment and believing in the power of RTT at the same time. We are using their own suggestibility to hasten and deepen their healing. It's so limiting and reductive to think we have to choose between alternative healing modalities and conventional medicine. The truth is that there is a great deal of mystery in how humans heal themselves, and while we gain so much from the rigor of science and innovation of modern medicine, that is not the be-all and end-all of what we know or how we heal. Using techniques like command cell therapy and the healing vortex isn't a stand-in for surgeries, medications or procedures like IVF, they are a powerful complement to them. And growing bodies of science are increasingly proving what many mystics and ancient cultural traditions have long known to be true. Your thoughts influence your reality. I'm sharing my story here because I hope it teaches you that you have this power too. I call it the bounce back factor. The idea that we all have the capacity to be like a big rubber ball. I believe in it when a relationship ends, when a career or job ends, and certainly when you get an illness too. So much of that bounce is down to your belief in expectations. Do you imagine yourself springing back up into the air with grace and ease after something difficult occurs? Or do you see yourself stuck forever? When life is hard do you get up every day and tell yourself that life always changes and you are participating in creating that new reality? Or do you simply accept that life will always be bad? So much of RTT is changing the image in people's minds and giving them a new sense of agency over their own life. It's in telling them that they get to choose how to answer that question and whether and how they bounce back. We all walk around telling ourselves stories every day. So why not choose to tell ourselves the story that gives us everything we've ever dreamed of?

CHAPTER 12. RTT for me As I mentioned in the introduction, this book is not intended to be a how-to manual for RTT. There are all kinds of insights and connections that RTT trainees learn to make on their training courses, not to mention hours of practice, observations, supervision, and other course requirements that can't be adequately captured in an audio book. However, there are some RTT techniques that you can safely and effectively use on yourself. These techniques are especially helpful when used as a kind of rapid and regular intervention to problems you're already aware of that may resurface now and then. In the following list, you will find some techniques that have already been introduced in the previous chapters, as well as some additional ones that work well as a self-practice. I want to be clear that are not suggesting the techniques that follow can replace therapy, but rather they can be used for issues such as boosting your confidence and self-esteem, stopping binging, or reversing a habit of procrastination just to name a few. You can think of these like brushing your teeth. You still need to go to the professional hygienist or the dentist every so often, but if you brush regularly, your dental issues will be far less severe. You can use these techniques along with the others previously presented at the end of each chapter to transform your daily life. Role function purpose intention RFPI If there is some behavior or habit that you keep repeating and would like to get rid of, say binging or constantly being late for appointments or calls, ask yourself what role function purpose or intention that behavior is serving. If you're unsure, ask yourself how you feel when you're doing it. As that can be a clue, do you feel loved? Do you feel important? Do you finally feel filled up or enough? Do you feel distracted or rewarded? Once you know what emotional purpose the behavior is serving, you can begin to see how it's not fit for the job. If you think binging on sugar makes you feel safe and loved, replace it with something more appropriate, such as connecting with your partner or calling someone in your family. Often our worst habits or behaviors are trying to fulfill an emotional purpose that they are not fit for. Installing the cheerleader Often it's hard to find the praise we need out in the world. Even if we do hear what we want from the people we love, we don't always believe them. We may assume they want something from us or we may not be able to let it in. That's why providing your own praise is so powerful. Our mind believes what we tell it, good or bad, so you might as well supply it with the good. It's helpful to personify this praise as a person, cartoon character, or my personal favorite, a cheerleader. Make it something silly or over the top so you have a strong image in your mind. Then allow them to praise and cheer for you as you go about your day, especially if you're going through a hard time. No win is too small and not worth cheering and praise. Even if it feels silly, providing yourself with this encouragement on a regular basis will have huge impacts on your life. If it helps you, have your cheerleader cheer out loud while you look in the mirror. You may feel silly at first, but once you see how it gradually shifts your inner dialogue, you won't want to stop. Dialogue with the herter. As we know, it's very often the case that our issues stem from being mistreated by a parent, bully, carer, or other authority figure very early in our lives. Of course, this is not our fault, but it is our responsibility to make sure that this early trauma or hurt does not ruin the rest of our lives. Unfortunately, it's not always possible to confront the person who hurt us and ask them to make it right. But fortunately, we don't need them to. We can use dialogue with the herter instead, as I did with Ryan. Counterintuitively, this can provide more healing than dialogue in with the actual person who hurt the client, because in the real life scenario, the client may not hear or say what they need to hear. Marissa, what else would you like to ask your father or tell your father? Ryan, why couldn't you speak with me after I told you I was gay? Marissa, be the father. When your son came to you and told you he was gay, why couldn't you talk to him? Ryan as his father, I was ashamed. Marissa, he was ashamed of you and ashamed of himself. Be the father and tell Ryan why it was so hard for you to love anyone. Ryan as his father, because nobody ever loved me. Marissa, so there's your answer. No one ever loved him. At the end of dialogue with the herter, the client may forgive the parent or herter and feel love for them and from them, but not always. Both outcomes are okay. Sometimes I also use this technique to help a client create healthy aboundries with a destructive parent who is still in their life. At home, you can use dialogue with the herter to imagine having a truth-telling conversation with a person who hurt you. Usually this is a conversation that would be difficult or impossible to have in real life, such as with a parent who has passed away or a teacher or authority figure who abused you as a child. The script is simple. You directly tell the person what they did and how it hurt you, and you don't sugarcoat it. So you might say, Mum, I need to tell you something. You hurt me. Your inability to love me properly affected my whole life and stopped me from experiencing love for so long. I didn't deserve that. It wasn't my fault. It was yours. Many people respond to the idea of this technique by saying, I can't possibly say that to my mother. My culture doesn't allow that or her life was so hard I don't want to make it worse. But the beauty of this technique is none of that matters. This is not about the herter. It's about you. This imaginary conversation can bring a healing effect that a real conversation with all of its potential complexity, misunderstanding and defensiveness cannot. Once you have stated how the person hurt you and explained the effect it had on your life, you ask them a question. Why did you do that? Why didn't you love me as much as my brother? Then you can sit in another chair facing where you were sitting before and imagine what they might say in response to your question. For example, I didn't love you because my mum didn't love me or I didn't love you as much because I really wanted to have a boy to please my husband who I thought would leave me if I had another daughter. Say whatever feels the most true to you, even if it's not what the herter would actually say. Finally, you finish with the most healing question of all. If you could do it over, what would you do differently? Here you can reply in the voice of the herter saying what you want to hear or you wished would have happened. Often that answer is as simple as, I would have loved you and let you be who you are. I'm so sorry. You're doing it to get resolved for yourself. Often the things the herter says to you in this imaginary conversation are things they would never be able to say to you in real life. That is okay. The point is validating and reinforcing that your feelings are valid. You were mistreated and you deserved to be loved perfectly. Furthermore, it's you asserting that you refuse to carry around the guilt, shame, blame or pain any longer. The wonderful thing is that when people become the herter and take on the energy of the parent or whoever, they often embody a spirit of compassion for both themselves and the herter, acknowledging that everyone did their best however flawed. Even if you are skeptical of this technique, I urge you to try it because I've seen it transform people so many times. Three things wrong with you. As we learned in Ryan's chapter, most people's issues connect to one of the three beliefs people commonly have. I'm just not enough. I'm different so I can't connect. What I want isn't available to me. It's really useful to figure out which of these applies to you. It's possible that it's more than one. Once you figure that out, you have to go to work counteracting them. When you think you're not enough, you have to challenge that statement. I am enough. I always will be enough. Remember, you're not the size of your thighs, your bank account, what you look like or your weight. What you are is enough. When you say that every day, you're fixing the thing that's wrong with you. Use the audio recording I provided at the end of chapter 6 to reinforce this. When it comes to the second belief, I'm different and I can't connect. You have to realize that our greatest fear is to be different and whatever we look for we find. So stop looking for why you are different and start looking for why you're the same. It can be comforting to remember that we all operate on the same thoughts, beliefs and fears. Instead of repeating to yourself how different from others you are, make your statement of truth. I'm connecting and I have the same hopes and fears as everyone. Remember, the mind learns by repetition. It lets in whatever you tell it. Stop telling yourself the lie that you're different and you can't connect and tell yourself the truth. I'm the same as everyone and I can connect. If your fear is that you are different and that's everybody's great fear, then the very fact that you have it means you are connected to everyone else. Regarding the last belief, that's not available to me. You have to make a decision that everything is available to you. Love, success, health, wealth, joy, inner peace. Whatever you want is available to you. It may involve work to get it but it's available. By making that decision, you will start to work in the direction of what you want but you first have to believe you're worthy of it. That's not me. That's not me is so simple and powerful in its declarative nature. It is at once a fact and a transformation. It interrupts a childlike or outdated belief. Often, an RTT therapist will use this when a story a person has about themselves is extremely out of date and no longer serves them. For example, Jasmine believed that candy and junk food was where she gained love which was why she was obsessed with binging on sweet foods in secret as an adult, fueling her bulimia. But that belief is when she gained as a small child after her parents divorce when her dad would give her candy and treats in secret. It's no longer relevant to her. Marissa, I want you to say that isn't me. I don't want candy in my cupboard. I don't need to hide candy or anything anywhere because I don't need that to cope anymore. Jasmine, that isn't me. I don't want candy in my cupboard. I don't need to hide candy or anything anywhere because I don't need that to cope anymore. Marissa, say I don't need sugar, sweets of a children and I'm an adult. I don't need that and I don't want that. Jasmine, I don't need sugar. Sweets of a children and I'm an adult. I don't need that and I don't want that. This technique is particularly helpful if you're trying to get rid of behaviors or issues that were severe in your past. So if you experienced an extreme lack of confidence or you feel unlovable and you're feeling it creeping up again, interrupt it and say, that's not me because that can never be me ever again because that will not be me ever again for the rest of my long gorgeous life because be sure to complete that statement using powerful words and a strong voice. Do it several times adding words and phrases like because I'm not three years old. I don't depend on my parents. I don't live that life anymore. I am free now. The Triple A's of feeling. This is a process you can take yourself through when you're experiencing difficult emotions. Perhaps ones that are causing you to act or behave in ways you'd like to stop. First, you become aware of what you're feeling and try to name it. Second, you accept those feelings as valid and don't try to minimize or second guess them. Lastly, you articulate those feelings out loud. Remember, your job is to feel your feelings until they no longer need to be felt. So when you can be aware of, accept and articulate that you, for example, feel jealous of your sister, that feeling will leave you faster. It's when you say, I should not feel jealous. I'm a a bad person for being jealous, that the feelings stubbornly stick around. Once you have done this, you can add in feelings that are more up to date and based on current information. This is a helpful tool that clients can use even when they're not in a hypnotic state. It mimics the process of RTT in hypnosis and fast-track sit to problem-solve things that can come up in life. Remember, the sooner you acknowledge your difficult feelings, the sooner they will pass and allow you to feel something else. Becoming a loving parent to yourself. This is an extraordinary technique we've explored several times and in several manifestations throughout this book. It can be done in a sequence with the following two techniques, upgrading the child and merging the child or on its own. When performing it for yourself, you simply imagine holding an infant-aged version of yourself in your arms and then say these magic words, I'm becoming a loving parent to you now.
